candidates.title: Evaluation of state-of-the-art large language models in interpreting veterinary emergency biochemistry panels: a multidimensional comparative study with GPT-5.2, Claude Opus 4.5, and Gemini 3 Pro
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored as clinical decision-support tools; however, their performance in interpreting veterinary emergency biochemistry has not been systematically evaluated. This study aimed to evaluate the clinical adequacy of state-of-the-art LLMs in interpreting biochemical analysis results from cats and dogs. Biochemistry specialists developed 255 emergency biochemistry cases (156 dogs, 99 cats) covering 33 clinical scenarios. The cases encompassed high-mortality emergency situations. Each case included a complete biochemistry panel, blood gas analysis, preanalytical indices (hemolysis, lipemia, and icterus), and species-specific reference ranges. Three LLMs, GPT-5.2 (OpenAI, December 2025; 400K-token context window), Claude Opus 4.5 (Anthropic, November 2025), and Gemini 3 Pro (Google, November 2025; 1-million-token context window), were evaluated based on six criteria: primary diagnosis accuracy, syndrome classification, critical value identification, clinical reasoning, preanalytical awareness, and urgency assessment. The weighted composite score was calculated on a scale of 0–100. The results showed that Claude Opus 4.5 had the highest average composite score (76.3 ± 9.9), followed by GPT-5.2 (74.9 ± 10.8) and Gemini 3 Pro (68.7 ± 10.2). GPT-5.2 had the highest primary diagnosis accuracy (2.27/3). Claude Opus 4.5 performed best in critical value identification (77.1%), clinical reasoning (2.30/3), preanalytical awareness (1.48/2), and urgency assessment (1.00/1). The weakest criterion was preanalytical awareness for GPT-5.2 and Gemini 3 Pro. The performance ranges of the models were 66.9–74.9 for cats and 69.6–77.9 for dogs. While state-of-the-art LLMs showed promising performance in veterinary medicine, expert-level proficiency was not achieved for preanalytical interference assessment or complex multi-organ syndromes. LLMs should be positioned as auxiliary clinical decision support tools alongside experienced clinicians, and future research should investigate retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) combined with veterinary-specific fine-tuning to enhance performance.

candidates.title: Selective stabilisation of social norms by Chinese large language models: a multidimensional analysis of marriage and fertility orientations
candidates.abstract: This study examines normative orientations in Chinese large language models (LLMs) by analysing how generative systems construct and stabilise meanings around marriage and childbearing in AI-mediated communication. Drawing on a multidimensional framework, we analyse five domains: institutional legitimacy of marriage, necessity of childbearing, intergenerational obligation, social and civic value, and gender roles. Using a repeated elicitation design, we collect 89,600 responses across 28 Chinese LLMs and develop a Weighted Stance Score (WSS) to capture both directional orientation and response consistency. Results reveal a structured pattern of normative bias. LLMs consistently endorse marriage and childbearing, while exhibiting more heterogeneous orientations on gender roles, intergenerational obligation, and civic responsibility. Cluster analysis identifies distinct normative profiles, especially in how models frame family formation and demographic issues as private or collective concerns. Among open-source models, model scale is positively associated with more traditional orientations, although this relationship varies across dimensions. These findings suggest that LLMs exhibit selective stabilisation at the level of generated discourse, consistently reproducing certain normative orientations while expressing greater heterogeneity across more contested domains. Beyond the substantive case of marriage and fertility, the study demonstrates how multidimensional and consistency-sensitive auditing can reveal the patterned value orientations embedded in generative communication and contributes to understanding LLMs as active discursive intermediaries rather than neutral information tools.

candidates.title: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) for Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is the mainstream technology to improve the mathematical reasoning ability of large language models, but evaluation protocols across papers are not unified, and low-sampling and high-sampling pass@k metrics often yield inconsistent conclusions, and there is a lack of systematic review of the evaluation practice. Focusing on the core issue of evaluation completeness, this paper systematically combs three RLVR technical routes: outcome supervision, process supervision, and verifier-free, analyzes the principles of representative algorithms, summarizes the experimental results of public papers, and designs a structured coding scheme covering 9 fields. The 9 representative papers are coded one by one from the aspects of technical route, base model, sampling scale, and training configuration. Statistics show that the current RLVR field is deeply in the dilemma of fragmentation of evaluation protocols: the caliber of evaluation indicators is incompatible with each other, high-sampling evaluation data are scarce, and there are obvious differences on whether low sampling can expand the reasoning boundary. The disclosure of key hyperparameters such as temperature and KL coefficient is scattered and unsystematic, and the horizontal comparison lacks a common foundation. Based on this, this paper proposes a structured coding analysis framework to provide a unified benchmark for the horizontal comparison of evaluation results for subsequent research.

candidates.title: Multimodal Large Language Models for Construction Safety Inspection
candidates.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have drawn more research interest in construction safety inspection recently due to their capacity to integrate visual understanding, language understanding, and reasoning. In this paper, a survey is conducted to review the recent research on MLLMs in construction safety inspection, covering techniques, datasets, evaluation, applications, and limitations. The current studies primarily utilize prompt-based adaptation and in-context learning, domain-specific fine-tuning, and knowledge-augmented reasoning to enhance the performance of MLLMs in the construction domain. Applications of MLLMs in construction safety inspection include hazard detection and localization, safety inspection, visual question answering, assistance, and report generation. From the current studies, it can be found that MLLMs can be used to perform flexible and interpretable analysis for construction safety inspection with the assistance of domain knowledge and prompts. Nevertheless, the limitations of MLLMs in construction safety inspection are still present, such as poor visual grounding and spatial reasoning, lack of domain knowledge, lack of large and balanced datasets, and uncertainty of application in real-world scenarios. For the future work, it is recommended to enhance multimodal grounding, construct a larger and more balanced dataset in the construction domain, integrate safety regulations in a trustworthy manner, and perform human validation systematically. MLLMs have great potential to be applied in construction safety inspection; however, they can be used as decision aids rather than replacements for safety inspectors at present.

candidates.title: Large Language Model-Driven Misinformation Detection: Methods, Trustworthiness Evaluation, and Challenges
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have offered a new path for misinformation detection, but the reliability of model-generated auxiliary information and the applicability of detection results in new scenarios have yet to be verified. Some representative studies and related methods have been classified into three types in this paper: content-driven, context- and relation-driven, and knowledge- and evidence-driven methods. Factual reliability, generalisation reliability and the reliability of explanations and evidence are introduced. According to the comparison of previous experiments, semantic augmentation, simulation of user behaviour and logical reasoning can all improve the detection rate in specific circumstances; however, the level of improvement differs depending on the dataset and model parameters. This suggests that method selection should depend on the available information and the specific detection scenario, rather than classification scores alone. Based on the above results, this article analyzes and evaluates issues such as data contamination, synthetic data bias, and external evidence reliability, providing reference for the selection and evaluation of detection methods.

candidates.title: HalluciNOT: execution grounded detection and targeted repair of symbolic drift hallucinations in large language model reasoning
candidates.abstract: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit a specific and previously undercharacterised reasoning failure we term symbolic drift hallucination: an intermediate variable within a multi-step computation graph silently receives an incorrect value, which then propagates through all subsequent derivations to yield an output that is linguistically coherent, structurally sound, and numerically wrong. This failure mode is invisible to existing single-signal verifiers because the model’s verbally stated answer and its generated symbolic code both carry the same corrupted value, causing them to agree on an incorrect result. We present HalluciNOT (Hallucination Neutralisation via Obligatory Testing), a three-stage post-hoc framework comprising: a constrained Program-of-Thought equation generator that enforces structural integrity of symbolic outputs; a guarded drift detector that compares sandboxed execution results against the ground truth, closing the detection gap that defeats verifiers restricted to the model’s own outputs; and a targeted Reflexion repair loop that isolates the corrupted variable for re-grounding. Because the repair stage accepts a candidate only when it lies within $$10^{-6}$$ of the ground truth, a strictly tighter bound than the $$10^{-3}$$ tolerance of the evaluation metric, the framework cannot convert a correct result into an incorrect one; the guarantee is unconditional, independent of repair quality, and independent of detector calibration. This framework is scoped to contexts where ground truth is available at inference time, such as automated grading, evaluation pipelines, and educational platforms with known answer keys. Evaluated on 600 samples across three benchmarks (GSM-Hard, SVAMP, and MAWPS, each with $$n = 200),$$ HalluciNOT achieves accuracy of 92.0%, 99.5%, and 100.0% respectively, with gains of +23.0, +4.0, and +5.5 percentage points over the LLM baseline. A three-condition evaluation shows that execution grounding and targeted repair recover disjoint failure sets: execution grounding corrects 46 baseline errors while introducing 6 new ones, and repair corrects a further 25 cases that the PoT-Only variant does not recover, including all 6 execution-induced regressions. An ensemble investigation reveals that symbolic drift hallucinations are deterministic given the prompt, establishing that inconsistency-based sampling cannot address this failure class and motivating pre-execution magnitude analysis for recall improvement. candidates.title: Beyond Language Form: Semantic Understanding in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: The rapid development of large language models has led to a profound and challenging question: is it enough to prove that these models understand the meanings of language if they perform well in linguistic tasks? This paper argues that the success of the task alone does not fully demonstrate its complete semantic understanding ability. Based on the analysis of the distinction between linguistic form and meaning proposed by Bender and Koller and the evidence of statistical shortcuts, this paper explores why successful task performance does not necessarily demonstrate semantic understanding. However, since human-produced text reflects interactions with the world, models trained based on such data might develop conceptual relations and even reference connections through human language practices. Nevertheless, these abilities are still not enough to constitute a complete understanding. In this way, semantic understanding should be regarded as a multidimensional structure, covering conceptual relations, reference, contextual interpretation, and communicative intention. Each of those dimensions should be assessed separately through tests that exclude surface-level shortcuts, rather than inferred from overall task accuracy. The resulting question is which aspects of semantic understanding language models can demonstrate, and what evidence would be needed to assess each of them.

candidates.title: Automated annotation of verbal communication skills in objective structured clinical examinations using a retrieval-augmented large language model: a pilot comparison against human coders
candidates.abstract: Introduction Communication and history-taking skills are core clinical competencies, yet their assessment in Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCEs) is constrained by examiner workload and rater subjectivity. We evaluated whether a retrieval-augmented large language model (LLM) pipeline can reproduce trained human annotation of Calgary-Cambridge communication elements in OSCE encounters. Methods Two hundred OSCE encounters of medical students with standardized patients were annotated against a nine-element Calgary-Cambridge codebook, eight of which were retained for transcript-based annotation. Forty encounters seeded a vector database of exemplars; the remaining 160 encounters were transcribed with Whisper and segmented into phrases, and each phrase was classified by an LLM (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) supplied with retrieved exemplars but not with the surrounding dialogue. Pipeline output was compared segment by segment with a human reference that had been completed before the pipeline was run; for each element, sensitivity, precision and F1 were computed from matched label counts, with micro- and macro-averages across elements. Results Across the 160 encounters the coders assigned 4,408 labels and the pipeline 4,775, of which 3,532 matched (micro-averaged sensitivity 80.1%, precision 74.0%, F1 0.77; macro-averages 78.0%, 71.2% and 0.74). F1 was highest for gathering information (0.89), providing structure (0.83) and verbal empathy (0.83), intermediate for opening the discussion (0.75), understanding the patient's perspective (0.70) and reaching agreement (0.69), and lowest for sharing information (0.65) and providing closure (0.62). Precision was below sensitivity for every element. Conclusion A retrieval-augmented LLM pipeline reproduced human coding of structured communication behaviors with high agreement, but agreement was lower for sharing information, closing the encounter and the more interpretive elements, and the pipeline consistently assigned more labels than the coders. Because neither a human-human agreement ceiling nor a comparison without retrieval was available, these findings are preliminary. Evaluation that reports precision alongside sensitivity for each element, accounts for dialogue context and is anchored to a measured human ceiling should precede any use of such pipelines in medical-education assessment.

candidates.title: An evolutionary framework for automatic optimization benchmark generation via large language models
candidates.abstract: Abstract Optimization benchmarks play a fundamental role in assessing algorithm performance; however, existing artificial benchmarks often fail to capture the diversity and irregularity of real-world problem structures, while benchmarks derived from real-world problems are costly and difficult to construct. To address these challenges, we propose an evolutionary automatic benchmark generation framework that leverages a large language model (LLM) as a generative operator, termed the LLM-driven evolutionary benchmark generator (LLM-EBG). In this framework, the LLM serves as an evolutionary operator that generates and evolves benchmark problems within a flexible, expressive representation space. As a case study, we generate unconstrained single-objective continuous minimization problems represented as mathematical expressions designed to induce significant performance differences between a genetic algorithm (GA) and differential evolution (DE). Experimental results show that LLM-EBG successfully produces benchmark problems in which the designated target algorithm consistently outperforms the comparative algorithm in more than 80% of trials. Furthermore, exploratory landscape analysis reveals that benchmarks favoring GA are highly sensitive to variable scaling, demonstrating that the proposed framework can generate problems with distinct geometric characteristics that reflect the intrinsic search behaviors of different optimization algorithms.

candidates.title: Visual sequence structure shapes in-context choices in vision–language models
candidates.abstract: Abstract Vision–language models (VLMs) process ordered images, yet how unlabelled visual context shapes their subsequent choices remains unclear. Using paradigms adapted from human visual statistical learning, we tested three commercial VLM deployments across five experiments without task-specific weight updates. Structured image sequences increased target choices relative to frequency-matched shuffled sequences in two deployments, although invalid responses in the third prevented the preregistered pooled test. Target choices also increased with successor strength. All three deployments preferred previously encountered image orders. Crucially, reversing image order within three-image chunks reduced forward-order choices from 98.7% to 1.9%, with the test question and alternatives unchanged. However, choices involving unseen exemplars of familiar visual categories varied markedly across deployments. These findings show that unlabelled visual sequence structure can systematically influence VLM choices, and underscore the importance of visual context history for understanding and evaluating multimodal models.

candidates.title: Targeted Use of N-Grams and Semantic Cohesion in Large-Scale Qualitative Data Analysis with LLMs
candidates.abstract: There have been ongoing concerns about the interpretive variability in qualitative research in which Large Language Model (LLM)-driven automation has created opportunities and risks for non-expert individuals to access, analyze, and disseminate insights in recent data-intensive contexts. Hence, a targeted modeling of the discourse patterns that can help identify the right semantic features that can provide interpretive clarity and replicability is the need of the current research landscape. This article systematically examines experiences of LLM-assisted analysts and the extent to which these experiences help them navigate textual ambiguity and establish meaning consistency. We developed a hybrid analytical pipeline, named N-Gram Salience and Semantic Cohesion Lens (NGSC-Lens), by using the AntConc corpus tool and regression, where we extracted lexical bundles, and further compared the effects of semantic cohesion clusters with the n-gram frequency distributions on the meaning-making accuracy of annotated corpora. For the proposed framework, the phrase bundles reported during the observation period ranging from 5-token sequences to 11-token sequences (a distributional summary of bundle frequency is included) is analyzed and a total of 173 sequences were depicted more relevant to the selected professional discourse contexts. Findings argue that emergent interactional norms, coupled with computational reproducibility concerns and the semantic anchoring power of the lexical bundles and the clustered cohesion units, continue to reshape the inferential frameworks of qualitative analysts and push some coding approaches to transition from inductive exploration into targeted prediction and pattern emergence from corpus data. Our improved bundle coherence rate for these tasks, particularly those with a low agreement baseline, may present scalable pathways for appropriate discourse-aware analysis.

candidates.title: Risk assessment for onshore wind power projects using retrieval-augmented LLMs and semantic clustering: a text mining study in China
candidates.abstract: Purpose Wind power projects are vital to the global energy transition but exposed to multifaceted risks, with relevant knowledge largely embedded in lengthy and unstructured professional documents. This study aims to systematically identify and assess dispute-related risks in onshore wind power projects using such data. Design/methodology/approach This study analyzed 3,031 judgment documents concerning onshore wind power projects on the Chinese mainland. An large language model (LLM)-enhanced text mining framework was developed to integrate deep learning-based text classification, retrieval-augmented LLM extraction, semantic clustering, and Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution-based risk evaluation. Findings Fifty risk factors were identified across seven categories: environmental complexity, technical complexity, participant capability deficiencies, contract deficiencies, opportunistic behavior, process deficiencies, and performance deficiencies. Compared with most internal project risks, external environmental risks occur less frequently but tend to have more severe economic consequences. Considering both frequency and severity, equipment-related technical and supply-chain risks emerge as most critical, while opportunism-related execution risks, contract-related risks and financial risks also rank prominently. Originality/value As an exploratory effort to investigate onshore wind power project risks using large-scale ex post evidence from project disputes, this study advances understanding of the risk landscape and the relative criticality of individual risks affecting multiple stakeholders across the project lifecycle. The proposed LLM-enhanced framework offers an effective and scalable approach for extracting structured risk knowledge from unstructured professional records. The findings provide insights for more differentiated risk management and dispute prevention.

candidates.title: Precision-Aware Learning Rate Transfer Across Block Count in LLM Post-Training
candidates.abstract: The post-training of pretrained large language models, including supervised finetuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR), is very sensitive to the learning rate, and tuning it through grid search is costly in both computation and memory. In this work, we propose \textbf{TipSweep}, a method to transfer the learning rate across the number of trainable transformer blocks. To do so efficiently, we search for the best learning rate by training only the last $k_0$ blocks (in our experiments, typically $k_0=1$), and provide scaling rules that predict the optimal learning rate when training any set of $k$ blocks, including when $k=L$ (the full transformer). Across experiments with models ranging from 1 to 7 billion parameters, we observe that the optimal learning rate follows precision-dependent scaling rules: the optimal rate scales approximately as $k^{-1}$ with float32 (FP32) master weights, but as $k^{-1/2}$ when updates are applied directly to bfloat16 (BF16) weights without a master copy. We explain both rules using an analytical model that accounts for update rounding, under assumptions supported by profiling experiments. Finally, we develop two prototypes of the learning rate search for a 6.7-billion-parameter model. The first fits the search on a single consumer GPU with 16 GiB of memory. The second speeds up the search on a high-end GPU by evaluating all candidate learning rates in a single pass over the data, so that a five-candidate search takes about half the GPU hours of one full-depth ($k=L$) run.

candidates.title: Post-Training Agents for Long-Document Reasoning
candidates.abstract: Professional documents are a long-context workload that retrieval-style benchmarks do not capture. In a ten-domain enterprise collection, a task's evidence is spread across a source document of median length 27 pages (mean 48.8, maximum 873); a third of tasks rest mainly on charts, drawings, and maps; and 70.9% require two or more reasoning hops. We post-train Kimi-K2.7, an open-weight foundation model, at its full context window on 1,465 expert-authored tasks with atomic rubrics from that collection, training rank-32 adapters with one round of privileged-context on-policy self-distillation followed by two rounds of rubric-reward reinforcement learning. We render each PDF as text for training and as extracted text plus selected page images at evaluation. The smoothed RL training reward rises from 0.37 in the first tenth of the run to 0.67 in the last. On the 100-task GDP.pdf holdout, served in a 262,144-token window, strict pass (all rubric criteria met) more than doubles after the second round, from 11.0% to 24.5%, with gains across input lengths up to 240K tokens. Mean tokens generated stay flat (9,803 to 9,733), so the gain does not come from longer outputs. GPT-5.6 Sol's leaderboard strict pass is 30.7% at a measured 3,422 tokens. On 220 out-of-domain GDPval tasks, where the model runs as a long-horizon tool-using agent, mean rubric reward rises from 0.571 to 0.746 after the third round and zero-credit tasks fall from 54 to 10, while messages per task fall 18%, from 70.9 to 58.2. In paired trajectories, the third round replaces a context-thrashing retry loop with one up-front check of all sources, and verification extends from checking that files exist to checking what they contain. We argue that long-context evaluation of agents should report accuracy jointly with tokens and turns, and that datasets of long documents should ship text and image renderings alongside each PDF.

candidates.title: Learning Heterogeneous Reasoning in Large Language Models: From Mode Compatibility to Local Bottlenecks
candidates.abstract: Post-training large language models routinely pools reasoning trajectories from diverse teachers or algorithms, yet it remains unclear whether standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can learn such heterogeneous strategies without explicit mode conditioning. We study the learnability and local bottlenecks of heterogeneous reasoning through a formal mixture formulation and controlled experiments. We first formalize the representational compatibility of the optimal autoregressive model with latent reasoning mixtures: the target next-token distribution weights modes by their prefix posteriors and concentrates on a single mode once alternative modes assign negligible likelihood to the prefix. In a verifiable symbolic graph-search environment with paired breadth-first and depth-first search trajectories, no consistent disadvantage is observed for unlabeled mixed SFT relative to homogeneous or labeled baselines under matched token budgets while preserving both modes. Scaling across 0.6B--14B models and data budgets largely eliminates global mode confusion, shifting the primary bottleneck to local state-tracking transitions. Because a local mistake affects the final outcome only when subsequent reasoning is sensitive to that step, we find that only a small fraction of local errors are outcome-determining \emph{Critical Reasoning Nodes (CRNs)}, and that single-step repairs at these nodes rescue failing trajectories across symbolic search and natural language benchmarks whenever the model has sufficient downstream competence to complete the remaining derivation. Our environment is open-sourced at https://github.com/Bowen1911/Symbolic_graph_env.

candidates.title: Evaluating Chunking Strategies for Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Homogeneous Academic Documents
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the factual reliability of large language models by combining generative capabilities with external knowledge retrieval. While extensively studied in open-domain and heterogeneous corpora, RAG’s performance in highly homogeneous and structured domains, such as institutional academic documents, remains underexplored. These document types are often lengthy, redundant, and formatted according to rigid institutional standards, posing unique challenges for information retrieval and semantic segmentation. This study systematically evaluates chunking strategies for RAG pipelines applied to Indonesian higher education documents, including curricula, syllabi, academic guidelines, and standard operating procedures. We compare fixed-length token-based chunking with varying sizes and overlaps to structure-based chunking aligned with logical document sections. All documents were preprocessed, embedded using IndoBERT-based sentence transformers, and indexed in ChromaDB. Retrieval effectiveness was assessed using Precision@k, Recall@k, and Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) with curated academic queries. Results indicate that smaller fixed-length chunks achieve higher top-1 precision, whereas structure-based chunks maintain semantic coherence and deliver superior recall across top-k retrieval. Integrating these retrieval strategies with LLaMA 3.2 and a Telegram bot demonstrates practical usability, providing accurate, context-grounded responses in real time. These findings highlight the critical role of chunking and top-k selection in optimizing RAG performance for structured, redundant academic corpora and offer guidance for designing knowledge management systems in higher education.

candidates.title: Sparse Hodge Preference Optimization: Fine-Tuning Language Models toward Alignment beyond Transitive Preferences
candidates.abstract: The growing adoption of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which leverages pairwise preference data, reflects its great success in fine-tuning large language models to align with human expectations. It directly optimizes the policy from human preferences without explicit reward modeling or the complexities of reinforcement learning-based approaches. However, the classic DPO relies on the Bradley--Terry sampling model and cannot effectively capture intransitivity or cyclic structures in aggregated human preference data. In this article, we propose Sparse Hodge Preference Optimization (SHPO), a preference optimization algorithm that augments DPO with a sparse antisymmetric curl residual motivated by the combinatorial Hodge decomposition. We prove that SHPO strictly enlarges DPO's hypothesis class on comparison graphs containing at least one triangle, under some mild regularity conditions on the response representations. We further establish a theoretical guarantee for $\ell_1$-regularized estimation of the curl coefficients under fixed policy and representations. Qualitative studies on three preference datasets under the same QLoRA budget, SHPO-aligned LLM achieves satisfactory performances in preference accuracy, cyclic structure recovery, and GPT-4o-judged generation quality.

candidates.title: SHAKTI: Evidence-Grounded Conversational AI for Nutrition and Health
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) answer many diet and health questions but can state unsupported claims and cite sources that do not support them. We present SHAKTI (Smart Health Advisor for Knowledge-based Tailored Interventions), a conversational assistant that answers only from retrieved scholarly papers and exact food-composition data, and evaluate it with retrieval, generation, grounding, efficiency and contextawareness metrics. We indexed 484,368,086 OpenAlex works, searched exactly on a GPU for evaluation (10,065 NFCorpus, BioASQ, SciFact and PubMedQA questions) and through a compressed 230-million-abstract index in deployment. On 1,000 stratified questions, we compared single-shot, multi-hop, corrective and deep-research retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with Claude Sonnet. SHAKTI adds conversational query rewriting, USDA FoodData Central lookups, source-link checks and online verification of quotes and numbers. It was tested in 36 scripted conversational turns, a 248-question memory-depth test and a 38-question load test. Claims were checked by a Claude Opus judge against exactly the text the system saw. MedCPT reranking of hybrid retrieval gave the best MRR (0.21) and MAP@100 (0.14). Across existing RAG methods, faithfulness was 0.95-0.96, claim hallucination 0.5-0.8% and context precision up to 0.98; the deep-research agent answered 73.2% of BioASQ questions correctly. In conversation, SHAKTI reached a context-awareness score of 97.1%, faithfulness 95.5%, 1.9% unsupported claims, no contradicted claims and 229/229 working source links; it resolved references to the first question after 16 unrelated questions. An answer cost 14,716 tokens (US$0.06) with a median latency of 24 s. Large-scale retrieval with agentic evidence selection and mechanical verification yields auditable, low-hallucination nutrition answers.

candidates.title: From Local Errors to System Failures: Modeling and Benchmarking Error Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
candidates.abstract: In multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs), errors can propagate through intermediate messages and compromise final answers. However, outcome-based evaluation obscures how agents amplify, attenuate, or correct these errors. We propose Response-Aware Error Propagation among Agents (REPA), a structural model that connects measured local responses to system-level error propagation. REPA separately estimates input assembly and agent processing across multiple error channels, while theoretical analysis relates local modeling errors to endpoint prediction error. candidates.title: Automatic Occupational Coding through Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Annually 1.9 million deaths and 89.7 million disability-adjusted life years are caused by exposure to agents during work (e.g., welding fumes, silica dust, and noise pollution). To improve worker health, high-quality exposure assessments are crucial. Therefore, free-text job descriptions from large-scale occupational cohorts are manually standardized through occupational classifications and linked to hazardous exposures using Job Exposure Matrices (JEM). However, manual coding is slow, unreliable (i.e., 44-89% inter-coder reliability), and costly, due to i) short, ambiguous free-text job descriptions, ii) classifications containing hundreds to thousands of categories, and iii) the absence of gold standards. With 46%-79% accuracy, state-of-the-art automatic occupational coding tools achieve classification performance on human level. However, their performance drops to 17-26% on out-of-distribution datasets. Furthermore, their supervised architectures limit them to occupational classifications present in the training set. Consequently, JEM using other classifications are incompatible, leaving vital exposure-response associations unexplored. Our Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework, OPERAG, enables classification into any occupational classification without expert-labelled databases. It retrieves coding index information and combines this with Large Language Model-based classification. Validated on AsiaLymph's 36,062 real-world job descriptions, OPERAG achieved 42.6% occupational classification accuracy on the 4th coding level, substantially outperforming existing tools and approaching human coders' 51-56% inter-coder reliability. Using two JEM named ALOHA+ and SHOCK, 89.9-98.6% accuracy was achieved on exposure assessment. OPERAG approaches human-level, universal occupational classification, enabling efficient and effective large-scale exposure assessment to improve worker health.

candidates.title: When 1+1 $\neq$ 2: Benchmarking Civil-Time Reasoning in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Calendar arithmetic is non-linear. When 1:59 AM + 1 minute occurs during daylight saving spring-forward, the result is 3:00 AM, not 2:00 AM, as the hour is skipped. We introduce CivilTime-Bench, a benchmark for civil-time reasoning covering daylight saving transitions, non-hour offsets, date-line crossings, and ISO week boundaries. With 60,011 training and 10,500 evaluation examples under strict output-contract evaluation, we benchmark seven LLMs (six instruction-tuned models and Llama-3.1-8B base) and find: zero-shot exact match varies substantially across models, contract-aware prompting often improves format compliance but yields inconsistent accuracy gains, few-shot in-context learning provides model-dependent improvements, and fine-tuning achieves 74.6--86.6% EM on synthetic evaluation but only 36.6--45.2% on HumanTime-500 for models with valid results on both splits, highlighting substantial limitations in generalization. candidates.title: WeMM-Ecom: Advancing Multimodal Content Understanding for WeChat E-Commerce
candidates.abstract: We present WeMM-Ecom, a family of multimodal large language models that deliver frontier e-commerce capabilities while achieving state-of-the-art general-purpose performance at their respective scales. The family spans five sizes, from a 0.8B dense model to a 35B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. Our training pipeline begins with two-stage continued pre-training that progressively raises the proportion of e-commerce data within a diverse multimodal data mixture, followed by hybrid-thinking post-training that combines on-policy distillation and reinforcement learning to support both non-thinking and thinking modes. For evaluation, we construct a comprehensive suite of 28 e-commerce benchmarks (23 in-house and five open-source) covering eight business scenarios and complement it with 64 public general-purpose benchmarks. On the e-commerce suite, WeMM-Ecom-35B-A3B surpasses substantially larger open-source flagship models, including Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, HY4, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. On the general-purpose suite, every WeMM-Ecom model surpasses its similarly sized Qwen3.5 counterpart, with the lightweight variants (e.g., WeMM-Ecom-2B) showing clear advantages over leading lightweight models such as Qwen3.5-2B, MiniCPM-V-4.7-1B, and LFM3-VL-2B. Beyond benchmarks, WeMM-Ecom now powers hundreds of production use cases in WeChat, including catalog management, multimodal product search, and livestream commerce, serving billion-scale requests per day. We publicly release all model weights and detail our data curation, training recipe, and benchmark construction to facilitate future work on domain-specialized multimodal models. We have released the model weights and code to facilitate future research at https://github.com/Tencent/WeMM-Ecom.

candidates.title: Training-Free Interventions for Hallucination in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: A frozen language model can give a wrong answer because a fact is unavailable, a reliable passage is ignored, or an unsupported claim survives generation. We review 116 works on inference-time hallucination intervention and its foundations. We trace the development from retrieval and controllable generation to methods that act on input evidence, token scores, internal representations, completed claims, or the decision to answer. For each family we compare its source of evidence, model access, preparation cost, and the task on which a correction can be established. For activation steering, we distinguish estimating a subspace from applying a state-dependent edit and separate interventions on the prompt from those on the generated prefix. Published comparisons show why faithfulness to a source, factual correctness, informativeness, and answer coverage must be measured separately. Applications in time-sensitive question answering, document synthesis, and visual grounding identify when source authority, evidence availability, or capability preservation limits a reported gain.

candidates.title: Test-Time Latent Computation to Improve Visual Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Recent work on Large Language Models (LLMs) suggests that reasoning capabilities can be enhanced at test time not only through longer token-level reasoning traces, but also through additional computation in latent space. This raises a natural question for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs): can additional computation in latent space improve visual perception at test time? In this work, we first verify that MLLMs contain stable reusable layers that can be re-forwarded at inference time without disrupting normal generation. Based on this observation, we propose \textbf{Lo}ok \textbf{Ba}ck in the \textbf{L}atent \textbf{S}pace (\textbf{Lobals}), a training-free decoding method that identifies the contiguous layer window with the strongest visual-token attention and re-forwards through it, allowing the model to revisit visual evidence in latent space. We demonstrate that this latent-space revisit strategy can improve MLLMs' performance across diverse multimodal settings, including general vision-language tasks, visual hallucination tasks, and vision-centric tasks.

candidates.title: SuSi-RAG: A Hybrid Graph RAG for Equipment Maintenance
candidates.abstract: In the manufacturing domain, equipment maintenance tasks depend on expert knowledge. Their documentation is often stored in heterogeneous formats and sources. The enhancement of LLMs with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is promising for bridging the scattered knowledge, but traditional vector-based RAG shows weaknesses with two characteristics which are common in real maintenance queries: complex causal chains and cross-domain synthesis. To address this, we propose SuSi-RAG, a hybrid Graph RAG solution, that matches a user query and each maintenance record using subgraph similarity. This work shows an in-use system: SuSi-RAG has run on an active Bosch production line for more than eight months, handling 10,664 question-answer interactions and demonstrates upper bound answer accuracy of 96.25% (confirmed error rate 3.75%). In a proof-of-concept, SuSi-RAG improves top-1 retrieval accuracy from 61.5% to 96.2% and expert-rated answer quality from 44.9% to 84.1% against a vector-based baseline. We present an integrated operational feedback loop to update SuSi-RAG.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation in the Agentic Era: Tradition, Present, and Prospect
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) couples frozen language models with external, updatable knowledge, so that generation is grounded in retrieved evidence rather than in parametric memory alone. This work maps RAG in the agentic era by joining them on a single lifecycle axis, from offline indexing through pre-retrieval, retrieval, post-retrieval, and orchestration over these stages. It treats indexing and orchestration as first-class components and agentic workflows as a paradigm of their own, and it covers the agentic work that has appeared since those reviews. Beyond these components, it covers evaluation, applications, and the questions that remain open for future exploration. From tradition to present and beyond, this work systematically reviews RAG from a perspective of the agentic era.

candidates.title: Rethinking the Evaluation of Contrastive Decoding for Hallucination Mitigation in Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Contrastive decoding (CD) mitigates object hallucination in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by contrasting token distributions under different conditions to adjust token scores. However, existing generative and discriminative benchmarks primarily measure final task scores, which can be confounded by candidate filtering, changes in generation trajectories, and response biases, making it difficult to isolate the effects of the underlying contrastive adjustments. To address these limitations while complementing existing evaluations, we introduce CONCOR (Contrastive Correction Evaluation), a controlled benchmark that directly evaluates the competition between ground-truth and different types of hallucinated candidates using the Contrastive Grounding Margin (CGM). CGM also enables analysis of directional consistency, composition, and reliability of contrastive corrections. Our evaluation reveals that existing CD methods exhibit distinct correction behaviors: some consistently favor ground-truth candidates, whereas others produce strong corrections but also introduce more errors. Crucially, these differences help explain their contrasting responses to increased contrast strength, which improves some methods while degrading others. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating the contrastive correction itself, rather than relying solely on final-output performance, and CONCOR provides a controlled and interpretable framework for understanding and improving CD methods for hallucination mitigation.

candidates.title: Reading the Tea Leaves, Again: Can Large Language Models Predict Language Model Training Runs?
candidates.abstract: LLM agents now propose research ideas and run the experiments that test them, but they train every run to its end, whereas a researcher reads a run's configuration and the beginning of its curve and stops the runs that show no promise. Reading a run this way takes more than describing or implementing a training method: it takes knowing what a design choice does to a run. We build Tea Leaves to measure this knowledge on 682 real training runs across pretraining, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning (RL): a forecaster sees the first 20% of a run with its configuration, description, and code, and predicts the rest. Across 11 LLMs and a range of forecasting baselines, the strongest LLMs match or exceed the best curve fitter on smooth loss curves (skill 0.66 against 0.62) and lead on noisy RL reward curves (0.43 against 0.13). What bounds every forecaster is what the log carries: on sparsely logged community runs all methods lose most of their skill, and none reliably flags a failing run in advance. Beyond the curve, information helps and effort does not: related runs in the prompt cut the error on loss curves by 39%, and knowledge of training dynamics lets the strongest LLMs order all 36 pairs of runs that differ by a described code change, which the early curves do not separate, whereas tools add little. This knowledge can be learned from logged runs: a small open model trained on public runs matches the best LLM on loss curves. Applied to the progress curves of research agents, the same reading ranks tasks by their remaining headroom, although for a single agent run it does not improve on the last value. We release the benchmark, the trained readers, and their training data to test and train LLMs' understanding of training and to help research agents decide which runs deserve their compute.

candidates.title: Quantizing Diffusion LLMs under Parallel Decoding: Commitment Risk and the Parallelism Tax
candidates.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) are served with accelerated decoders that cache context and commit, in one step, every masked position whose confidence clears a threshold. Yet post-training quantization of dLLMs has so far been calibrated and evaluated under fixed-step samplers without caching. We study W4A4 quantization under the deployed decoder and find that the decoder determines both where quantization harms accuracy and what it costs. Irreversible errors enter chiefly through forced commitments, made when no position clears the threshold: they are a minority of commitments but carry most quantization-induced flips. Quantization also levies a parallelism tax, extra forward passes per response: by compressing top logit gaps, it pushes positions below the threshold while leaving predictions largely intact. We propose DECAL, which reweights layer-wise calibration by a commitment-risk prior measured on the deployed decoder, and an argmax-preserving commit temperature that recovers the tax. On LLaDA and Dream, DECAL attains the best average accuracy among W4A4 methods, with lower run-to-run variance than the closest existing calibration method.

candidates.title: PCC: Pivotal Channel Compensation for Layer Pruning of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Treating independent layers as the minimal pruning unit allows layer pruning to efficiently eliminate many redundant parameters and achieve high compression rates. Layer pruning has become a promising and prevalent structured pruning technique for large language models (LLMs). However, multi-layer removal can lead to significant performance degradation for LLMs. Although some works have explored various compensation methods for pruned layers, they are inefficient and costly. Observing that the expression of a large proportion of information is concentrated on a small number of pivotal channels, we propose a novel post-pruning compensation method for layer pruning, called pivotal channel compensation (PCC). PCC can achieve significant performance improvement by compensating for a small number of channels through learnable linear transformations at the pruning interface. Besides, we propose a new evaluation metric, called channel-wise average performance improvement (CAPI), which can measure the efficiency of channel-wise compensation. Our experimental results across various LLMs demonstrate that PCC can achieve significant and consistent improvements and high CAPI on language modeling and zero-shot question answering for the state-of-the-art cross-layer and consecutive-layer pruning methods. Compared with existing compensation methods, PCC can achieve competitive results with fewer additional parameters and less training cost.

candidates.title: MH-RAG-DIVE: Dynamic and Cost-Efficient Multi-Hop RAG Evaluation via Tree-Cached Dialogue Simulation
candidates.abstract: Quality assessment is essential for determining whether changes to a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system improve or maintain its performance. However, existing evaluation approaches often rely on single-turn or single-hop interactions and therefore do not capture the complexity of multi-hop, multi-turn conversations. We introduce MH-RAG-DIVE, a dynamic interactive user simulation framework designed to evaluate RAG systems in more complex multi-hop and multi-turn settings. The framework extends RAG-DIVE with a Context Discoverer, which identifies documents that can be combined to generate multi-hop questions within an ongoing conversation. To address the high computational cost of dynamic user simulation, we further introduce a Conversation Cacher, which reuses turns from previous evaluation runs while preserving the dynamic nature of the evaluation. We evaluate the framework across six distinct RAG configurations and compare its results with the original RAG-DIVE evaluation and the static, human-created CLAPNQ dataset. Our experiments show consistent performance trends across the evaluation approaches, while the more complex multi-hop and multi-turn setting exposes additional challenges for RAG systems. Furthermore, the Conversation Cacher substantially reduces token consumption, demonstrating its potential to make dynamic evaluation more cost-efficient. Finally, we apply MH-RAG-DIVE to an industrial RAG system with domain-specific data, demonstrating its applicability to real-world evaluation scenarios. Overall, our results show that the proposed approach provides a more complex and cost-efficient framework for evaluating RAG systems. All code and experimental data are publicly available in our GitHub repository (https://github.com/Daniel-Innsbruck/MH-RAG-DIVE).

candidates.title: Automated Call for Action: RAG-Based Environmental Law Enforcement Screening System
candidates.abstract: Environmental law inspectors face a structural issue in identifying potential violations from data: they often do not have the capacity to deal with large volume of data present in the emission events. A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline then retrieves facility-specific permit conditions and generates event reports and a period report with an investigation recommendation. Across 74 events from March 2025, plant-aware re-ranking reduced reports citing the other plant's conditions from 58.1% (hybrid retrieval) to 0% by rule-based plant labels, while maintaining high RAGAS and LLM-judge metrics. GPT-5-mini performed comparably to GPT-5.1, whereas GPT-5-nano scored lower on legal grounding and legal faithfulness. In an evidence ablation, removing air quality (AQ) data changed judge scores and period recommendations most; citation overlap changed only slightly under any removal, and removing complaint details had no measurable effect. This suggests a need for rules and guidelines that link complaints to incidents and permit conditions, so that community reports can count as evidence. The results support screening of events that may need further investigation. Design implications for involving environmental service experts are derived.

candidates.title: What Quality Engineers Need to Know About Generative AI: Structured Data Extraction
candidates.abstract: In this expository paper, we explain how quality engineers can use large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) for structured data extraction. To ensure the accuracy of our AI-driven structured extraction, human evaluators validated the results. In the first app, four reviewers assessed information extracted from 30 recall notices using two models, with 98.6% of the 720 field-level ratings judged fully correct. In the second app, 21 authors evaluated information extracted from 45 of their arXiv papers. All paper summaries were rated mostly correct or correct, although the evaluations identified problems with some classification fields and mathematical expressions. candidates.title: RoboUniverse-10K: Toward the Scaling Era of Agentic Robotics via Real-to-Sim Environments
candidates.abstract: Agentic Robotics, in which foundation models act as coding agents to control robots through executable programs, has emerged as a compelling paradigm for embodied intelligence. Yet unlike software engineering, where massive executable environments power post-training, robotics remains constrained by small, manual benchmarks and in-distribution evaluation. Each runs in an isolated, Harbor-compatible harness that hides privileged states and grading logic to mirror real-world sensing. From the same pipeline, we hold out 500 unseen tasks to establish RoboUniverse-Verified, an expert-verified zero-shot benchmark. Evaluating 11 closed- and open-source models reveals a huge gap: frontier models reach 85.8\% success, while open-source baselines lag at 2.6\% to 10.0\%, bottlenecked by low-level grasping, deformable-object manipulation, and post-contact physical control. Finally, we collect about 17K multi-turn trajectories totaling 0.79B tokens with GPT-6 Astra and perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, yielding RoboUniverse-35B-A3B. Our model achieves substantial zero-shot gains on RoboUniverse-Verified, lifting the success rate from 0.8\% to 21.2\%, while achieving zero-shot task completions across LIBERO-MAX, RoboCasa, RoboTwin 2.0, and a real Franka arm. candidates.title: Learning Teacher Output Preferences from Final Responses for Reasoning Distillation
candidates.abstract: Many large language models (LLMs) use chain-of-thought (CoT) to solve complex problems, but hide their CoT traces to prevent reasoning capabilities from being distilled. While recent studies have shown that hidden CoTs can be reconstructed, existing methods typically require training a separate attacker for each target LLM. This paper studies model-agnostic CoT reconstruction, aiming to reconstruct hidden CoT traces from arbitrary target LLMs using only input prompts and visible final responses. We propose Final-Output Preference Learning (FOPL), which trains a single reconstruction model that generalizes to unseen LLMs without target-specific adaptation. To achieve this, the reconstruction model must learn which reasoning patterns match a given final response without knowing the target LLM's identity. We address this using preference optimization, training the reconstruction model to prefer native CoTs over synthetic alternatives for the same question and final response. By learning these preferences from LLMs with accessible CoTs, the reconstruction model learns to distinguish reasoning patterns based on visible responses. Experiments show that reconstructed CoTs capture distinct reasoning patterns across LLM families, including a family unseen during training. Moreover, students trained on reconstructed CoTs match or outperform those trained on native CoTs across several reasoning benchmarks.

candidates.title: Audio-Visual Rearrangement

Moreover, we propose a framework that integrates a motion-aware spatial audio module into an audio-visual large language model to encode spatial cues from the spoken request and update them as the agent moves. We further incorporate auxiliary supervision for speech understanding, spatial audio perception, and visual grounding through multitask instruction tuning to improve action prediction. Experiments establish baseline performance in both seen and unseen environments, laying the groundwork for future research on embodied intelligence and human-robot interaction. candidates.title: mini-psych-agent: Evaluating Human-Like Behavior in LLM Agents through Interactive Psychological Environments
candidates.abstract: A Large Language Model (LLM), its harness, and the test-time compute budget jointly determine its behavior. Consequently, the same underlying model, embedded in different agentic workflows or allocated different amounts of test-time compute, can exhibit markedly different performance. Psychologists face an analogous challenge when evaluating human performance: the same person may behave differently under different incentives and levels of deliberation. Psychological tasks therefore provide an ideal testbed for studying such behavioral variation. However, when adapted to LLMs, these tasks are typically text-transcribed, replaying fixed, language-rendered experiments as static prompts. This format is ill-suited to agent evaluation, where actions can alter future observations and task states. Conversely, although dynamic environments are prevalent in the evaluation of LLM agents, they rarely ask whether the resulting behavior is human-like. Here, we bridge this gap by transforming psychological tasks into dynamic environments in which agents can interact and by using a learned human-policy model to evaluate how compatible the resulting behavioral trajectories are with human behavior. Across these environments, we find that this compatibility varies with an LLM's agentic configuration and the psychological task, and that memory raises it mainly by making choices more predictable rather than more human-like. These findings motivate a more holistic evaluation of LLM agents in psychology-inspired environments, accounting for both the backbone model and its agentic scaffold.

candidates.title: WASP: Continual Weight Adaptation for Streaming LLM Personalization

Specifically, WASP achieves this by training a shared hypernetwork that maintains a compact user representation and outputs adapter weights in a single forward pass. As new interactions arrive, WASP updates this representation without reprocessing full interaction history, enabling continual adaptation with per-update costs independent of history length. Experiments on personalization benchmarks and chronological interaction streams show that WASP sustains high-quality personalization over long horizons under fixed compute and storage budgets. Together, these results support efficient streaming personalization and facilitate privacy-preserving on-device deployment.

candidates.title: Verifying the Outputs of PDE Solvers: From Finite Elements to Neural Surrogates
candidates.abstract: Physics simulation outputs increasingly come from solvers that no expert inspects, such as third-party packages in automated pipelines, programs written by large language models (LLMs), and learned surrogates. In earlier work on cardiac pulsed field ablation, we proposed that solvers return a certificate with their answers. The certificate consists of an admissible potential and an exactly charge-conserving current, and a small independent checker turns it into guaranteed error bounds against a written specification of the physics. Here, the same checker verifies the outputs of other solvers on the same problem. Specifically, FEniCSx computes both fields and receives the same bounds as our own solver. Five plausible bugs in a correct solver, one of them about 0.2% from the true impedance, all converge and pass a grid convergence study, yet the certificate rejects or refutes all five. Of three solvers written by LLMs, one is correct and certified to 0.1%, and one never solves the equation but converges. Neural networks that predict the coefficients of a reduced basis emit admissible fields and receive valid per-prediction bounds, at most 0.0021% wide inside their training range and 0.3-25% wide outside it, where 90% conformal intervals cover none of 14 tests. Untuned Fourier neural operators with free nodal outputs receive valid but uninformative bounds. On a uniform grid, interpolation onto the certificate grid limits them, and on the certificate grid, thin cells turn small nodal errors into large energy errors. Energy-norm training narrows the certified interval tenfold, and projecting the nodal-loss outputs onto the reduced basis narrows it by two to four orders of magnitude, still uninformative. The guarantee concerns the stated model and holds for any output, wherever its input lies. It is informative only when the output is accurate in energy on a grid that resolves the problem.

To overcome this, we propose a generation-based black-box framework that infers context-induced information gain from targeted token discrepancies. We introduce a budget-constrained auditing regime, building on the empirical observation that the membership signal is highly sparse and concentrated in a few highly informative tokens. We formalize this sparsity, showing why uniform sampling needs many more samples than a policy that targets informative positions. Empirically, our approach achieves state-of-the-art black-box separation accuracy while needing about 3x fewer queries than uniform position sampling. Finally, we apply this methodology to closed frontier models, exploring its capacity and limits in surfacing potential training data overlaps on commercial APIs.

LPF succeeds on a suite of model organisms with hidden behaviours (8-14B parameters), and also surfaces naturally occurring hidden behaviours in open-weight models (27-35B parameters). They were more promising for recognising emergencies early: given only demographics, chief complaints, risk factors and red-flag answers, the best model reached an AUROC of 0.87. candidates.title: TriSegAgent: Context-Efficient 3D Annotation with MLLMs via Tri-Planes
candidates.abstract: Interactive segmentation models turn a few clicks into a segmentation prediction across domains, so annotators only decide where the prediction still needs correction. Annotation thus becomes a loop of inspecting the prediction and clicking again. Each step of this loop is a visual judgment, which suits general-purpose multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents. In this work, we focus on letting these agents run this loop on 3D volumes. However, the MLLM in such an agent takes only 2D images as input, so the agent must observe the 3D volume in 2D. Since the loop calls the MLLM many times, this observation must be token-compact enough to keep every call cheap, yet informative enough to show error regions in the 3D prediction. We meet both needs with tri-planes, the three orthogonal planes that cross at one point in the volume. We show, both theoretically and empirically, that tri-planes are context-efficient yet keep sufficient detail to show error regions in the 3D prediction. Building on tri-planes, we introduce TriSegAgent, an MLLM agent that refines the 3D prediction iteratively. Within the agent, the MLLM only judges the prediction on tri-planes, while a visual harness turns each judgment into a 3D action in code. To make the loop reliable, the harness places each click at an exact voxel in the volume and checks whether to accept the 3D prediction. To evaluate the agent, we build a diverse benchmark of 690 regions of interest (ROIs) from 35 public medical datasets across three imaging modalities. With frontier MLLMs, TriSegAgent reaches an overall Dice about 10 points above the strongest baseline, and its lead is even larger on targets below 3 cm. With flash-level MLLMs, it outperforms a recent 3D segmentation agent built on a frontier MLLM.

candidates.title: Transport-Safe Evaluation of LLM Agents: Trajectory-Dependent Judge Error and Anytime-Valid Auditing
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are often ranked by an LLM judge whose error rates are measured once and reused for every agent. The corrected success rates can then be biased when the judge's errors depend on the trajectory and agents differ in the trajectories they produce for successes or failures. We derive the exact asymptotic bias and give a chain of checks from identification to simultaneous ranks. On a four-agent semi-synthetic benchmark, a scalar correction with oracle calibration has maximum bias 0.245 and mean pointwise coverage 0.016, and never recovers the full ranking (0/250 replications). Augmented inverse-probability weighting (AIPW) with a uniform or a design-aware random audit keeps the maximum bias below 0.003, with mean pointwise coverage of 0.939 and 0.950. In a 48-cell stress test, effective target support rises only from 0.209 to 0.805 as calibration grows from 600 to 4,800 labels, while audited AIPW keeps a mean absolute error of 0.018-0.020. Without calibration support, or with judge dependence within an externally justified bound, we report valid bounds or sensitivity sets and carry them into rank sets. An e-process confidence sequence stays valid, for a stable target, under predictable adaptive auditing and arbitrary stopping.

candidates.title: Trallie: from Free-Form Text to Structured Data with LLMs
candidates.abstract: Trallie is an open-source framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to perform information extraction (IE) from natural language sources with or without user guidance. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on extensive labeled datasets or domain-specific training, Trallie enables the conversion of unstructured data into structured formats with minimal or no representative examples. The framework is designed with three key objectives: (i) reducing manual annotation by harnessing prompt-based zero-shot and few-shot capabilities of modern LLMs, (ii) flexibly parsing diverse document formats (i.e., HTML, PDF, TXT, and JSON), and (iii) improving accessibility for non-expert users by automatically inducing schemas from document collections, which can then be refined for extraction. We evaluate Trallie with open-weight LLMs on FDA 510(k) documents and on movie and university websites from SWDE. It outperforms previously reported systems when the target attributes are provided for text extraction and is competitive when it must discover attributes for the schema automatically. candidates.title: TamperCert: A Benchmark for Detecting Text Tampering in Degree Certificates
candidates.abstract: Degree certificates play a critical role in high-stakes decisions such as university admission, immigration, and hiring. The issuing institution vouches for the holder, so a forged certificate may let its bearer pass these checks. Degree certificate forgery is increasingly prevalent. Yet, many assume that it is easy to spot. Reported cases show otherwise: in 2024, the business school of the University of Hong Kong found that about 30 master's students had enrolled with forged academic credentials. Few studies have looked at how to detect forged degree certificates, partly because public benchmarks are scarce. We present TamperCert, a benchmark built from 400 real degree certificates issued by 38 universities. Each certificate was subjected to 11 publicly available tampering methods to alter the holder's name and further processed with four additional post-processing techniques, resulting in over 20,000 forged images. We evaluate 13 detectors, a commercial multimodal large language model (MLLM), and detectors trained on TamperCert.Our findings reveal that no detector is reliable for every tampering method. Consequently, a determined forger may still evade detection. Moreover, the commercial MLLM misses most forgeries made by general-purpose generative models, and post-processing, such as resizing an image or photographing it with a camera, severely degrades detection.

candidates.title: Semantic-aware Decoding for Diverse Text-to-SQL under Schema Ambiguity
candidates.abstract: Real-world text-to-SQL systems often face schema ambiguity, where a question can map to multiple plausible schema elements. To support downstream disambiguation, SQL generation systems should include diverse interpretations among their top-k predictions. However, large language models (LLMs) typically favor a single interpretation, producing highly skewed outputs. We propose Semantic-aware Logit Adjustment (SLA), a training-free decoding method that promotes diverse SQL generation by adjusting token logits based on semantic similarity between schema elements. Unlike prior approaches that rely on reasoning-intensive prompting or task-specific fine-tuning, SLA is efficient, model-agnostic, and easy to deploy. Experiments show that SLA consistently improves interpretation coverage over standard decoding and remains competitive with existing diversity-oriented methods at substantially lower inference cost.

candidates.title: Self-Upgrading Embodied Agents
candidates.abstract: An embodied agent built on a language model goes to work with the weights it was given and keeps them for life. To get better, it needs more training, or reflection, memory, search or prompts that cost every step and are lost when the task changes. Editing weights by reasoning, weight-space programming, could end this, but has stayed with models that only reason or relied on a far larger commercial model. We introduce the self-upgrading embodied agent, to our knowledge the first that learns from its own experience by upgrading its own weights on the job, between its tasks, with no training, no gradient, no reward model, no second model, no test-time scaling and no harness or prompt engineering. By day a 27B agent works in a household environment. At night it reads its record, finds many of its steps wasted on replies that reach the token limit before any action, traces the habit to one direction in its hidden states, and rewrites one tensor of its weights. An agent that rewrites itself must first never break itself, so it is its own examiner: it tests every change against its unchanged self on practice tasks and keeps only what holds. When an edit holds, the next day it is a better agent, at the same cost per step: over thousands of held-out episodes, 48 fresh seeds a task, its one kept edit makes it complete significantly more tasks, in fewer steps, with fewer wasted and fewer tokens. This self-improvement is multi-round, stable and continual: through the nights that follow, the upgrade holds, without collapse. Of four sizes of its family, only the 27B agent does this. From here on, an embodied agent need not keep training and inference apart: as it works, it gathers its own experience and upgrades itself, with no separate pre-training or post-training and no human intervention. We believe this opens lifelong continual learning for robots: stable, continual, recursive self-improvement.

candidates.title: SAEPO: Sparse-Autoencoder-Guided Credit Assignment for Policy Optimization
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has demonstrated strong performance in improving large language model (LLM) reasoning, yet its credit-assignment signal remains coarse. Outcome verifiers provide scalable supervision by judging whether a completed response is correct, but they do not directly indicate which intermediate reasoning tokens contribute to success or failure. As a result, policy optimization can be inefficient, especially when training base models directly from sparse outcome feedback. In this paper, we introduce SAEPO, a Sparse AutoEncoder-guided token-level credit assignment method for outcome-supervised Policy Optimization. Rather than treating correctness only as a rollout-level (sequence-level) signal, SAEPO uses a pretrained sparse autoencoder (SAE) to build token-level semantic representations within reasoning trajectories; it scores each token based on the SAE concepts (e.g., penalizing wrong "final-answer" tokens but rewarding correct "reasoning-process" tokens), learned in an unsupervised manner, to achieve fine-grained credit assignment. SAEPO is a plug-in advantage-shaping module compatible with various policy optimization algorithms. We instantiate SAEPO with both GRPO and GSPO, covering token-ratio and sequence-ratio policy-gradient objectives, and evaluate SAEPO across three LLM backbones on six math and two code benchmarks. Empirical results show that SAEPO improves both the math and code benchmark averages over the matched baselines, with gains of up to 6.63% and 5.57%, respectively. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base, training curves also show faster early accuracy growth. Feature and token-level analyses suggest that the SAE-derived signal favors question-relevant concepts and reasoning tokens.

candidates.title: Revisiting Learning to Delegate: LLM Discovered Heuristics for Large-Scale Vehicle Routing
candidates.abstract: Efficient vehicle routing is critical to logistics and transportation, yet solving large-scale capacitated vehicle routing problems (CVRP) remains computationally challenging due to their combinatorial complexity. One approach to solve large-scale vehicle routing optimization is to identify promising subproblems and then optimize them using solvers. In this paper, we propose a framework of automatic heuristic design (AHD) in which a large language model (LLM) autonomously refines heuristics for selecting subproblems, enabling effective optimization of large-scale CVRP instances. Compared to prior approaches that train task-specific neural networks to select among heuristically constructed subproblems, our method discovers generalizable, interpretable LLM-generated heuristics to directly construct subproblems. Experiments show that our approach achieves comparable in-distribution performance while outperforming neural network-based policies on out-of-distribution instances with large-scale problems.

candidates.title: Revisiting LLMs as Context Engineers
candidates.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are used in more and more new tasks, context engineering becomes a fundamental method to efficiently steer LLMs by constructing instruction prompts or metadata without intensive training. A growing number of LLM context engineering (LCE) approaches automate the task by casting the LLM itself as the engineer that draws generalizable instructions or experiences from offline trials as context. Although these methods resemble how humans learn from experiences, it remains unclear \textbf{when and how} LLMs can engineer effective context from data. To answer the question, we first establish a benchmark composed of datasets with different reasoning patterns. We compared different LCE methods with different LLM families in 8B size, showing that there is no single winner for all tasks, even compared with simple baselines like chain-of-thought. Even when scaling model capabilities via more parameters or generation iterations, LCEs do not consistently boost existing performance. Across all datasets and models, the performance gains of LCEs are negatively correlated ($r=-0.5, p\le 0.05$) with the diversity of the failure modes of reasoning trajectories. Investigating how LCEs work, we find that (1) the improvement in instruction adherence can explain some success of LCEs; (2) one major bottleneck is whether LLMs can extract effective experiences out of natively diverse failures. Through this study, we uncover the limited capabilities of LCEs in abstracting principled contexts from diverse failure modes and understand how LCEs work, providing guidelines for future work.

candidates.title: RepoClean: Evaluating Coding Agents on Repository-Level Obsolete Code Cleanup
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong repository-level programming capabilities. However, as software evolves, repository code may become redundant or obsolete, increasing maintenance costs and potentially introducing functional issues. To evaluate this capability, we introduce RepoClean, a benchmark of 200 cleanup tasks from 34 popular open-source Python repositories. RepoClean is constructed by automatically reintroducing deleted code from real repository histories into newer versions, preserving current implementations and retaining instances where previously passing tests consequently fail. To restore existing functionality without new feature development, agents must use repository interfaces and cross-file dependencies to determine which historical code to remove and which implementations to preserve. Further analysis reveals that agents remove substantially less obsolete code when cleanup is not explicitly requested.
