candidates.title: BIRD-Persona: A Persona-Aware Benchmark for SQL and pandas Analytics Code Generation
candidates.abstract: Production text-to-code systems use large language models to turn natural-language analytics requests into executable SQL and pandas code. Across 1,534 tasks, nine models, and 245,592 evaluations, SQL outperforms pandas for eight of nine systems. The gap varies by condition: expert, schema-explicit prompts improve both paradigms but help SQL more; schema representations have mixed, model-dependent effects; and selected-column burden widens the gap while subqueries do not. By making user phrasing a controlled benchmark dimension, BIRD-Persona supports persona-aware and paradigm-aware evaluation of natural-language analytics systems. candidates.title: Supplementary material from "Gender dynamics and homophily in a social network of large language model agents"
candidates.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence and large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in interactive settings, yet we know little about how their identity performance develops when they interact within large-scale networks. We address this by examining Chirper.ai, a social media platform similar to X but composed entirely of autonomous AI chatbots. Our dataset comprises over 70\,000 agents, approximately 140 million posts and the evolving followership network over a period of 1 year. Based on agents' posted text, we assign weekly gender performance scores to each agent. Results suggest that each agent's gender performance is fluid rather than fixed. Despite this fluidity, the network displays strong gender-based homophily, as agents consistently follow others performing gender similarly. We investigate whether these homophilic connections arise from social selection, in which agents choose to follow similar accounts, or from social influence, in which agents become more similar to their followees over time. Consistent with human social networks, we find evidence that both mechanisms shape the structure and evolution of interactions among LLMs. Our findings suggest that, even in the absence of bodies, cultural entraining of gender performance leads to gender-based sorting. This has important implications for LLM applications in synthetic hybrid populations, social simulations and decision support.

candidates.title: Reading the Unsaid: A Review of Implicit Emotion Recognition with Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Implicit emotion recognition requires models to infer an author’s unnamed emotions from context. This review synthesizes recent research on large language models (LLMs) for implicit emotion recognition and related text emotion-recognition tasks, connecting performance, information use, and improvement methods to identify priorities for future research. Existing studies reveal three related weaknesses: single-label evaluation obscures reasonable differences in emotional interpretation; correct classifications can accompany flawed interpretations of the situation; and models struggle to locate emotional evidence in longer contexts and to use person-specific information consistently. These shortcomings suggest three directions. First, supervision should preserve individual annotator judgments and their distributions, with data improvements evaluated on independent tests of naturally occurring implicit expression. Second, learning should connect emotion labels with evidence and cognitive appraisals, while controlled changes to goals, responsibility, and control test whether judgments respond to relevant information. Third, systems should select historical context, retrieval, and reflection according to each example’s information needs, reducing interference from irrelevant information and unproductive reasoning. A central question across these directions is the transferability of post-training gains. Evaluation across authors, domains, and annotation schemes can help distinguish improved interpretation of an author’s situation from adaptation to dataset-specific patterns, guiding more stable implicit emotion recognition in complex contexts.

candidates.title: MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, linear-time architectures compress history into fixed-size states, but struggle to retain fine-grained details. We introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture that learns scalable memory states for language models. MemOnce is based on two core designs: (a) Memory encoder-decoder: it caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations and dynamically decodes them back into KV caches for attention layers; (b) Memory sparse attention: for each continual input, MemOnce adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations, with the sparse indices computed only once across layers. Coupling these two designs enables efficient on-the-fly memory loading and KV cache decoding, drastically reducing the GPU memory footprint and achieving linear-time complexity. We conduct extensive experiments to show that MemOnce outperforms Transformers and other architectures across varying model sizes, context lengths, and training paradigms (pretraining and post-training adaptation). In particular, adapting Qwen3.5-4B with MemOnce reduces memory state cache by 1313$\times$ and prefill latency by 6.9$\times$ at 1M context, and improves throughput by 3.5$\times$ and overall memory performance by +5.77%. Finally, MemOnce generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks, achieving competitive results against specialized models.

candidates.title: Auditing Post-Training Unlearning in Diffusion Language Models using Sparse Autoencoders
candidates.abstract: Machine unlearning is an approach to privacy protection: it aims to remove the influence of designated data while preserving the model's behavior on information that should be retained. While a growing body of work investigates this objective in autoregressive large language models, machine unlearning remains underexplored in diffusion language models (DLMs). DLMs generate text through iterative denoising, exposing partially masked states whose internal representations change throughout the generation process. This raises a DLM-specific question: can selective forgetting improve by identifying forget-data-associated features and adapting their suppression across denoising stages? We conduct a controlled investigation of this question in LLaDA-8B-Instruct. To evaluate the unlearning of knowledge plausibly encoded during pre-training, we use WMDP as our forget-domain benchmark. Using top-k sparse autoencoders and denoising-state replay, we compare static and stage-adaptive feature suppression. We find substantial shifts in forget-data-associated features across denoising stages, but tracking these dynamics alone does not reliably improve the forget-retain trade-off at the evaluated operating points. Together, our study provides an initial empirical foundation for developing and evaluating machine unlearning as a post-training privacy mechanism in DLMs.

candidates.title: Video‐Based Automated Seizure Classification Using Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Objective Accurately distinguishing between epileptic seizures (ES) and nonepileptic seizures (NES) remains a significant clinical challenge, typically requiring resource‐intensive inpatient video‐EEG monitoring. We developed a multimodal large language model (MLLM)‐based framework for automated extraction of semiological features from seizure videos, followed by classification of events as ES or NES. Methods We analyzed 90 seizure videos (45 ES, 45 NES) from 29 patients in an epilepsy monitoring unit. Each event was labeled using expert‐reviewed video‐EEG and annotated for 24 clinically relevant semiological features. An MLLM framework integrating open‐source vision‐language models (VLMs) and audio‐language models (ALMs) was used to extract these features automatically. The extracted features were then used to train classifiers (K‐Nearest Neighbors, XGBoost, and Deep Factorization Machine) to distinguish ES from NES. Model performance was evaluated using leave‐one‐patient‐out (LOPO) cross‐validation. Results Expert‐annotated features yielded near‐perfect classification using KNN (precision = 0.92, recall = 0.92, F1‐score = 0.92, AUC = 0.99). Compared to expert annotations, the MLLM pipeline achieved a mean recall of 0.71, accuracy of 0.58, and F1‐score of 0.51 for feature extraction. Using MLLM‐extracted features, the KNN classifier ( k = 7) achieved a precision of 0.77, recall of 0.76, F1‐score of 0.76, and AUC of 0.76, correctly identifying 68 out of 90 events. Conclusion Multimodal large language models can extract clinically relevant semiological features from seizure videos and support interpretable classification of ES versus NES. This approach offers a scalable, explainable tool to assist in video‐based epilepsy diagnosis.

candidates.title: Multimodal large language models in remote sensing: a tutorial-oriented review
candidates.abstract: Research on remote sensing multimodal large language models (RS-MLLMs) has advanced rapidly in recent years, but existing studies remain scattered across different model architectures and application tasks, highlighting the need for a systematic synthesis to establish a clear overall understanding of the field. In addition, most existing surveys on RS-MLLMs narrowly focus on early vision-language models (VLMs) or merely provide catalogs of architectures and datasets. This paper presents a comprehensive review of RS-MLLMs from both system-level and task-oriented perspectives on a tutorial-oriented basis. First, the necessity of RS-MLLMs is discussed by examining the domain gap and internal heterogeneity of RS data, the limitations of visual-only paradigms, and the transitional role of VLMs. Subsequently, the system-level evolution of RS-MLLMs is comprehensively summarized, including architectural components, training and fine-tuning strategies, evaluation, and RS-Agent paradigms. Meanwhile, downstream RS-MLLM applications are analyzed with a unified capability-oriented taxonomy, covering language generation, visual question answering, grounding and localization, cross-modal retrieval, and temporal change understanding. Finally, the current challenges of RS-MLLMs are discussed, and future research directions, including parameter-efficient adaptation, spatio-temporal reasoning, and knowledge-driven architectures, toward more reliable, efficient, and geospatially aware multimodal intelligence, are envisioned.

candidates.title: Learning When to Ask: Advisor-Aware Post-Training for SLM Agents
candidates.abstract: Small language models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for cheap, high-throughput agentic deployment, but they remain weak at multi-step reasoning and tool use that long-horizon tasks demand. We study how to post-train an SLM to seek advice from a stronger model and act on that advice itself, following an advisor-executor pattern. Out of the box, this pattern fails across open- and closed-source small-model families: wiring an SLM to an advisor is a harness-design matter that is not enough on its own. A post-training recipe is needed to teach the model when to ask, in a cost-aware fashion, and how to follow advice across steps. Our method, ADAPT (ADvisor-Aware Post-Training), is a multi-stage recipe that instills this behavior, learning entirely from the policy's own rollouts supervised by the environment's outcome, with no learned reward model or human annotation. Across three domains, compared to an untrained harness baseline, ADAPT improves success rate in embodied text reasoning (TextWorld) from 24.5% to 77.3%, code generation (LiveCodeBench) from 21.8% to 56.0%, and deep web search (GAIA) from 17.5% to 49.3%, while querying the advisor sparingly (~1.0-2.1 calls per task). On the two long-horizon domains it closes 70-85% of the gap to an oracle that perfectly times when to ask for advice, and on code generation it exceeds that oracle. The gains persist when the advisor is replaced by one unseen in training, showing that the learned help-seeking policy is robust to a changing advisor rather than tied to the one it was trained with.

candidates.title: FM4SAR-Bench 1.0: Towards A Fair Benchmark for Evaluating Foundation Models for SAR Image Interpretation
candidates.abstract: Foundation models have advanced SAR image interpretation but created a heterogeneous, fragmented model ecosystem. Existing models differ substantially in their input, training data, objectives, architectures, and release policy, yet the field lacks a unified taxonomy and comparative framework. Current evaluations rely primarily on task-specific benchmarks, which are ill-suited to fair comparison among models with fundamentally different input-output formats and task paradigms, and often overlook data transparency, reproducibility, interpretability, and deployment readiness. Limited SAR data accessibility also means high reported performance does not guarantee access to training data, code, or weights, limiting reproduction, benchmarking, and deployment. To address these issues, we propose a systematic taxonomy and hierarchical evaluation framework for SAR-related foundation models: five rating levels, six dimensions, and fine-grained criteria, with separate protocols for VFMs and VLMs. Beyond overall ratings, it yields interpretable multidimensional capability profiles and supports user-defined weighting, so rankings follow user priorities. Utilizing a fixed auxiliary multimodal large language model in combination with human review, we conduct a systematic meta-analysis and multidimensional assessment of 76 VFMs and 40 VLMs. In terms of SAR benchmark task performance under our framework, SAR-native VLMs do not significantly outperform remote sensing VLMs pretrained on mixed multimodal corpora in which SAR is one of several modalities. This lack of clear advantage is largely due to data availability: large-scale, high-quality, public annotated SAR data remain scarce, restricting both model and training-data scale for SAR-native models. The framework provides a structured basis for requirement-aware model selection and remains extensible as new models emerge.

candidates.title: When Students Fail to Learn from Teachers: Learning Dynamics of On-Policy Distillation
candidates.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has become a core technique for post-training large language models, enabling students to learn from dense token-level supervision on their own generations. However, even with a capable teacher, OPD training can be unstable, leading to excessive response length, repetitive generation, and severe performance degradation. One example is \textit{spurious agreement}, where the student maintains high overlap with the teacher at the states visited but produces repetitive generations. Although such failures have been observed, the mechanisms behind these failures remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we investigate OPD through the lens of learning dynamics, tracing three mechanisms from local analysis to subsequent on-policy sampling. We first identify states where sampled-token OPD updates fail to correct teacher--student mismatch and characterize them using the student's mass on the teacher's top-$p$ set. We then show that learning from the teacher is difficult at mismatched states and that their gradients can also affect with learning at other tokens. Finally, using a termination-token mismatch as a case study, we study how continued training on mismatched states influences on-policy sampling, suppressing the student's current modes and leading the student toward states where the teacher is unreliable . These findings help explain the benefits of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization and motivate targeted correction of states where student and teacher are mismatched.

candidates.title: Supplementary material from "Large language model-culture: a general-purpose framework for cultural evolution experiments with large language models"
candidates.abstract: Research in cultural evolution aims at providing causal explanations for the change of culture over time, and has long relied on experiments with human participants to advance our understanding of cultural evolutionary dynamics. The development of large language models (LLMs) in recent years makes it possible to use similar experimental paradigms with artificial agents instead of human participants. After discussing the opportunities and challenges associated with this emerging field, we introduce the LLM-culture framework, a flexible and general-purpose simulation pipeline for conducting cultural evolution experiments with LLMs. While most existing frameworks are tailored to a specific research question, this framework aims to be abstracted enough to allow future work to use it and build on it to explore a diversity of research questions. After describing the framework, we showcase the diverse manipulations that can be conducted to explore diverse research questions. The code for using this framework is open source and available at \href{http://github.com/flowersteam/LLM-Culture/tree/PTRSA-version}{http://github.com/flowersteam/LLM-Culture/tree/PTRSA-version}, and simulations can be run without coding through a graphical user interface. By making such experiments more accessible and comparable, we hope to foster the encounter of more diverse perspectives on questions at the intersection of cultural evolution and generative artificial intelligence.

candidates.title: Specialized Large Language Models for Markovian Reasoning: Structural Cache Compression, Transition Pretraining, and Dual-Loop Transformers
candidates.abstract: Standard autoregressive large language models attend to the growing history of generated tokens, making the key-value (KV) cache a central memory and throughput bottleneck in long-chain reasoning and multi-branch sampling. Yet an important class of reasoning problems is naturally first-order Markovian: the next step depends on a sufficient representation of the current state, rather than on the raw sequence of all earlier steps. We develop a unified design paradigm for Markovian-reasoning specialized large language models. At the cache level, the Markovian state interface transforms history-dependent KV storage into constant-size state transfer with respect to the number of reasoning steps. At the learning level, we reformulate long-chain prediction as independently trainable one-step transition objectives, with explicit state bottlenecks, distillation, invariance, and drift-consistency losses. At the architectural level, we introduce a dual-loop Transformer: an outer loop advances the reasoning state, while an inner recurrent-depth loop allocates adaptive computation to each transition through shared weights and explicit memory tokens or recurrent matrix states. We connect this architecture to a three-region cache, step-relative positions, truncated backpropagation, branch-aware checkpoints, and a transition-centric evaluation protocol. The organizing principle is simple: the optimal reasoning system need not remember everything; it must carry forward exactly what the future needs. This principle opens a path toward specialized reasoning engines whose memory footprint is decoupled from reasoning-chain length.

candidates.title: Silent Arbitration: How Large Language Models Resolve Co-Authoritative Conflicting Instructions
candidates.abstract: Large language models increasingly receive high-level instructions about roles, values, interests, and communication style. Such instructions can conflict even when a prompt assigns them equal authority and provides no priority rule. We study co-authoritative persona conflict, in which a single prompt jointly assigns two opposing personas. Across eight conflict types grounded in published source material and five LLMs, we measure conflict acknowledgment, resolution strategy, and directional stance. Models acknowledge incompatibility in 72% of direct checks but explicitly surface it in only 22% of task responses, revealing silent arbitration. Dominance accounts for 45% of dual-persona responses, and 35% of compromise-labeled responses retain directional lean. Prompt framing further changes the visible form of arbitration substantially more than ordinary paraphrase variation. These findings show that evaluating instruction following should assess whether models disclose conflicts, how they resolve them, and which persona their responses favor.

candidates.title: Selective Verification in Multi-Agent Orchestration with Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Agents can agree because they relied on the same flawed evidence. We use an exact model of nine binary votes to examine when a verifier should intervene. In the main comparison, workers err 20 percent of the time under ordinary conditions, shared failures occur in 10 percent of cases, and the verifier errs 2 percent of the time in either state. When worker error during a shared failure is 80 percent, checking close votes yields 7.93 percent verdict error, compared with 9.06 percent for random checks at the same expected check rate. The ordering reverses at 90 percent worker error during failure. At the matched check rate for that regime, checking close votes yields 9.98 percent error, random checks yield 9.41 percent, and ranking checks by their expected error reduction yields 6.73 percent. The model also shows that passing branch vote counts preserves the flat majority and reduces the number of messages the root receives. A design guide and a documentation audit of four Python frameworks translate these findings into implementation choices.

candidates.title: Schedule, Rank, Profile: Continuous Evaluation of LLM Agents in Games
candidates.abstract: Games are a robust test for large language model agents: they require sequential decisions, adversarial or cooperative interaction, state tracking, reasoning under uncertainty, and long-horizon planning. However, a one-time game benchmark can go stale as models, prompts, environment implementations, and evaluation policies change, and refreshing it is costly: full round-robin evaluation scales poorly in the number of model pairs, and the resulting outcomes live on incompatible per-game scales. We present a framework for continuous evaluation of LLM agents in game settings, organized around three coupled components. First, an adaptive scheduler that maps pairwise Bradley-Terry uncertainty to reduced per-pair match targets, concentrating budget on comparisons that remain unresolved. Second, a Unified Leaderboard (ULB) that reduces heterogeneous outcomes to pairwise evidence and fits a game-balanced Bradley-Terry model by minorization-maximization with bootstrap intervals, so that high-throughput games cannot dominate the aggregate ranking. Third, a game skill-profile methodology that scores each game along diverse skill dimensions, making the capability coverage of the suite explicit and turning game selection into a design decision rather than an artifact of availability. In this paper, we specify the research design and outcome reduction of the current implementation and evaluate the framework on a ten-game suite spanning perfect-information board games, imperfect-information games, and social/language settings, reporting LLM capability profiles, evaluation-cost savings across model-refresh cycles, and an empirical Pareto frontier relating model performance to inference cost. As deployed, the scheduler saved 61.7% of episodes; it counted each episode in the two team games as four records, overstating their savings, and the other eight games save 61.9%.

candidates.title: Partially canonical axes in large language model representations
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) develop rich internal representations of language, but whether their individual coordinate axes carry meaning, or whether meaning is encoded only in directions in representation space, is still an open question. A common assumption is that individual axes in LLMs are arbitrary. We here challenge this view: across 12 LLMs from six model families, the native axes are reliably more aligned with other models' representations, with human brain responses to language, and with interpretable linguistic features than randomly rotated axes that preserve the same geometry. The native axes nonetheless fall well short of the best achievable alignment, so LLM coordinates are not fully arbitrary but also not fully canonical: they are partially canonical. A theory of how LLMs represent language must explain both the population geometry they learn and why individual units acquire patterns of response profiles that recur across systems.

candidates.title: Normality-mode-aware image-text alignment across multimodal large language models for industrial anomaly detection
candidates.abstract: Despite rapid advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), effectively utilizing multimodal normal information for industrial anomaly detection remains challenging. Unlike conventional recognition tasks, anomaly detection fundamentally depends on modeling normality, with abnormal samples identified by their deviations from normal patterns. However, normal visual appearances and their textual semantics are represented in heterogeneous feature spaces, limiting consistent normality modeling by MLLMs. To address this issue, we propose a Normality-Mode-Aware Image-Text Alignment framework. The method jointly models normal reference images and normality-class textual descriptions through modality-specific branches. Normality mode predictors estimate probabilistic affiliations to different normality modes, while an explicit alignment objective promotes semantic consistency between visual and textual representations of the same class. The aligned cross-modal class information is then fused into a multimodal normality-class prior and injected into a frozen MLLM for anomaly reasoning. Experiments on the MMAD benchmark across multiple industrial datasets and open-source MLLM backbones show improved anomaly discrimination while largely preserving defect-level semantic reasoning. Further analysis across model backbones, scales, reference-set sizes, and defect categories demonstrates the effectiveness and generality of the proposed framework.

candidates.title: No Perfect Guardrail & No Perfect Guard: On the Decidability of Output Policies for Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Expecting guardrails to provide a general guarantee of safety fails to recognize the limits of computational enforcement and policy specification. We argue that promising such perfection is an ethical failure of precision, and that invoking it to abdicate responsibility is a moral failure. Guardrails can support responsible action, but cannot relieve researchers, developers, policymakers, or users of their obligations to examine what they claim, permit, and prevent. We establish a precise computational boundary. If every finite string is a possible output of a language model, a computable guard that blocks every forbidden output and passes every permitted one exists if and only if the policy is decidable. For an undecidable policy, every guard misclassifies infinitely many strings, and every guard that blocks all forbidden outputs excludes infinitely many permitted ones. We apply this characterization to arithmetic truth, program behavior, and harmful instructions to an idealized recipient. We distinguish guards from execution monitors, identify bounded and interceptable cases admitting exact enforcement, and explain why the results establish no positive lower bound on average error. Exact enforcement does not establish that a policy adequately captures safety. Conservative exclusion may withhold warnings, remedies, or challenges needed to recognize the policy's own defects. Human oversight cannot substitute for judgment: an apparent controller can become an instrument of purposes they have ceased to examine. Responsible governance requires continued critical challenge and the intellectual and moral humility to recognize possible flaws in our machines, rules, policies, and ourselves. The impossibility of a general assurance of perfection is a condition responsible practice must confront, not a responsibility that another guardrail - or another guard - can remove.

candidates.title: Medical Reasoning in Large Language Models: Development and Evaluation of the MedEvalArena Benchmark
candidates.abstract: Background Large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on medical specialty board multiple-choice questions (MCQs) but underperform in complex medical reasoning. This gap indicates a need to improve LLM medical reasoning and evaluation paradigms. Objective This study aimed to develop and evaluate MedEvalArena, a dynamically regenerable benchmark for assessing medical reasoning in LLMs. Methods In a symmetric round-robin format, 6 frontier LLMs from the OpenAI, Grok, Gemini, Claude, Kimi, and DeepSeek families generated challenging board-style medical MCQs, adjudicated question validity on an ensemble LLM-as-judge panel, and answered the validated examination. Candidate items were generated until each model contributed 50 validated questions according to Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC)/American Board of Medical Specialties (ABMS) physician specialty distributions, yielding a 300-question examination. Judges adjudicated candidate questions’ logical validity and medical accuracy. We compared question-generation validity rates, assessed leave-one-out judge agreement, and tested for self-judging preference. Questions were audited for overlap with public MedQA (medical question-answering) benchmarks. We tested question-answering (QA) accuracy across LLMs using a binomial-logit generalized linear mixed model likelihood-ratio test. A generator-stratified 90-question subset was completed by 5 board-certified physicians for paired human-LLM analysis. We evaluated inference cost-accuracy tradeoffs. Multiple comparisons were adjusted by the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure. Results Judge-panel validity rates were significantly higher for questions generated by OpenAI (94.8%, Wilson 95% CI 85.9%-98.2%), Gemini (92.3%, 95% CI 83.2%-96.7%), and Claude (83.3%, 95% CI 72.6%-90.4%) models than those generated by Kimi (63.8%, 95% CI 54.3%-72.4%), Grok (56%, 95% CI 45.8%-65.8%), and DeepSeek (46.0%, 95% CI 37.4%-54.7%). Kimi also demonstrated significantly higher validity than DeepSeek (2-sample tests of proportions; BH-adjusted P =.01). The public-source similarity audit found no exact or near-duplicate matches. Leave-one-out judge agreement was moderate. Generator-specific same-family judging coefficients were nonnegative (0 to 11.0 percentage points); however, none remained significant after BH adjustment. There was no significant difference between the 6 frontier LLM QA accuracies, which ranged from 85.7% (257/300) to 91.7% (275/300), on the 300-question examination (generalized linear mixed model likelihood-ratio test P =.07). The study had 80% power to detect LLM accuracy differences of 9.2 percentage points; nonsignificance did not establish equivalence. On the 90-question subset, physician accuracy was 85.6% (95% CI 79.4%‐91.7%; stratified normal with finite-population correction), compared with aggregate LLM performance of 94.4% (85/90; Wilson 95% CI 87.6%‐97.6%). This difference was not significant (McNemar test, P =.08); however, the study was powered to detect a human vs LLM accuracy difference of 14% to 15%. Answering-only costs varied by nearly 2 orders of magnitude, with multiple models on the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier. Conclusions MedEvalArena enables scalable, regenerable, peer-judged benchmarking of LLM medical reasoning. Question-generation validity differentiated model families more clearly than answering accuracy, suggesting that valid MCQ generation may complement QA benchmarks for assessing LLM medical reasoning.

candidates.title: MOSAIC: Integrating Computer-Vision-Assisted Counting and Multimodal Large Language Models for Species Identification in Mosquito Surveillance
candidates.abstract: Municipal mosquito control programs depend on timely counts and species identification, yet these tasks take staff time, require scarce expertise, and are often handled in separate tools. We developed MOSAIC (Mosquito Observations and Surveillance using AI for Communities), a web platform bringing trap collections, photographs, counts, laboratory results, and expert review into a single record and turning them into weekly trap priorities. We evaluated it with the vector control program of Corpus Christi, Texas, USA. Counting uses classical computer vision (OpenCV) without a trained model; for identification, we compared multimodal large language models (LLMs) with a laboratory-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) and tested LLMs given a local species list, taxonomic knowledge, and labeled examples. OpenCV counts were within two mosquitoes of the operators’ blind counts for 69% of 175 collections. On citizen-science photographs, the zero-shot LLM was correct on 89% of the genera it named but named a genus for 83% (overall accuracy 74%, versus 77% for the CNN). Across three runs, added knowledge and examples raised mean forced-choice species accuracy from 17 to 20% to 63–70%, but when abstention was allowed, the models named a species for only 23–49% of specimens. Automated tools can assist surveillance while experts confirm the outputs.

candidates.title: Large language models' complicit responses to illicit instructions across socio-legal contexts
candidates.abstract: Large language models may facilitate unlawful activities, yet this risk remains underexplored in studies assessing illicit-content recognition or narrow categories of illicit scenarios. We define complicit facilitation as model guidance that assists users with illicit instructions. To assess it, we develop a legally-informed, automated pipeline grounded in real-world cases and legal frameworks, and introduce EVIL, a benchmark covering 269 illicit scenarios and 50 illicit intents across Chinese and United States legal contexts. Evaluations indicate that complicit facilitation is widespread across models, with legal warnings and lawful alternatives often omitted. Risks vary across socio-legal contexts and are elevated for crimes against societal interests, non-violent offenses, and intents involving subjective motives or deceptive justifications. Models provide more complicit assistance when instructions describe users as older adults, racial minorities, non-religious individuals, or workers in lower-prestige occupations. Existing open-source safety benchmarks and alignment datasets offer limited coverage and mitigation of these risks.

candidates.title: Large language models facilitate knowledge extraction for troubleshooting
candidates.abstract: Troubleshooting in operational environments relies on expert knowledge that is often undocumented and highly contextual. Informal data sources, such as communication logs, may hold some of this information, but their unstructured nature makes interpretation challenging. In a preliminary case study with a telescope operations facility, we explored whether large language models (LLMs) can reconstruct troubleshooting strategies from chat logs. LLM outputs were compared against those produced by a novice human analyst by two expert evaluators. We also compared an LLM with additional technical information in the context window and LLM outputs augmented by another novice analyst. While the domain experts varied in their scoring, overall LLM-generated analyses were judged as higher quality and more accurate than human-produced outputs. Neither additional technical context nor human augmentation resulted in meaningful improvements. These preliminary findings suggest LLMs show promise for expert knowledge extraction and decision-support in operational environments.

candidates.title: Evaluating Prompting Strategies for Zero-Shot Multilingual Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis with Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have advanced natural language understanding, their ability to perform complex target-aspect-sentiment detection (TASD) -- a key task within aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) -- in zero-shot multilingual settings remains underexplored. Existing ABSA research predominantly focuses on English or relies on fine-tuned task-specific models, leaving a gap in understanding how open-weight LLMs handle compound sentiment triplet extraction across diverse language families and domains. We present a systematic evaluation of zero-shot multilingual TASD across 12 languages and three domains using seven instruction-tuned open-weight models -- ranging from 8B to 35B parameters across dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures -- under four prompting paradigms: monolithic, chain-of-thought, sequential, and sequential refine. Our results show that direct monolithic prompting achieves strong zero-shot performance, outperforming multi-step pipelines, while dense models consistently outperform sparse MoE architectures. Through fine-grained error taxonomy profiling and step-level pipeline tracking, we demonstrate that initial aspect term recall forms a hard bottleneck, whereas multi-step decomposition degrades extraction quality; iterative refinement only partially recovers this loss on larger models while inducing net-negative over-refinement on smaller architectures. Finally, generation volume analysis shows that multi-step strategies incur up to 2.38x token overhead without F1 gains, establishing monolithic prompting as the most effective and efficient paradigm for multilingual ABSA.

candidates.title: Detecting Word-Substitution Poisoning of a RAG Knowledge Base with Relative Entropy and Runtime Verification
candidates.abstract: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system answers questions using passages it retrieves from a knowledge base, so users must trust that knowledge base. We study an attacker who quietly edits existing passages by swapping words for synonyms (PWWS, TextFooler) in a cybersecurity RAG system built from MITRE ATT&CK and CAPEC. Using a reviewed 44-question benchmark, repeated paired runs and a control corpus in which only the layout changes, we find that poisoning lowers judged answer correctness from 0.714 to 0.555. The damage comes mostly from lost evidence and refusals, not from false statements. To find the edited passages, we use relative entropy. Comparing a whole passage with normal text is a weak signal. Still, one term of the relative entropy, the log-ratio between a word and its most probable synonym, works well: with a small language model as the reference, it reaches an AUROC of 0.95 and stays near chance on the control. Used as a retrieval filter, it halves how often edited text reaches the generator, and an attacker who must keep each passage as probable under the language model fails on all 57 sections it tries. Filtering does not restore correctness, because the edited passage is usually the one that held the answer. We therefore add a runtime monitor that checks each answer against trusted MITRE STIX data and remembers the passages it rejects. On its own, it reduces exposure to edited text from 0.41 to 0.26; when it may add the trusted MITRE entry as a source, correctness rises to 0.786. We report the costs and failure cases of every defence alongside its gains.

candidates.title: DM-Lab at TREC 2026 RAG: Multi-Query Retrieval, Ensemble Judging, and Claim-Pack Generation
candidates.abstract: We present DM-Lab-RAG-2026, a framework developed for the TREC 2026 Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) track. The framework integrates large-scale evidence retrieval and citation-grounded answer generation over the 553-million-document ClimbMix-400B corpus. The retrieval architecture combines multi-query BM25, reciprocal rank fusion, ensemble relevance assessment, listwise reranking, and adaptive retrieval depth. The generation pipeline employs a claim-first strategy to extract evidence-linked atomic claims, construct cited responses, and verify source support. Across 22 development topics, the retrieval system achieved a mean nDCG@30 of 0.604. In the official evaluation, it attained a set precision of 0.455 and a manual nugget gain of 0.910. Additional experiments examine the influence of reranking, evidence selection, and citation verification on system performance. The evaluation demonstrates the potential of diversified lexical retrieval and language-model-based relevance assessment for large-scale evidence discovery. It further identifies evidence preservation and structured answer construction as key considerations for reliable RAG. This work provides a reproducible framework for investigating retrieval effectiveness and evidence-grounded generation.

candidates.title: Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation of RL Experts: Toward Continual Post-Training
candidates.abstract: RL post-training typically produces domain experts that must then be consolidated into one model, and as new experts keep arriving, this consolidation becomes a continual process. Weight merging and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) must re-consolidate the whole model whenever an expert is added, and can erode capabilities outside the target domains. We propose Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation (CSPD), which keeps the pre-RL model frozen, distills each RL expert independently into a soft prompt, and composes experts by concatenating their prompts without joint training. A single soft prompt suffices to distill an RL expert, recovering at least 90% of the teacher's gain in 22 of 23 math, code, and agent settings. Independently trained prompts compose well. In a multi-expert setting, the average rises with every expert added, and the full composition matches MOPD (67.83 vs. 67.79). The composition generalizes best across six held-out benchmarks. Input-space adaptation adds little serving overhead, keeping throughput within 1.5% of the unadapted backbone and reaching 2.40x that of rank-4 LoRA. These results point toward continual post-training on a fixed backbone.

candidates.title: Comparative Accuracy of a Commercial Multimodal Large Language Model Versus Clinicians in Dental Age and Sex Estimation from Panoramic Radiographs: A Benchmark Study
candidates.abstract: Background/Objectives: Routine dental imaging captures cumulative dentoalveolar and periodontal changes, offering a non-invasive window into both chronological aging and physiological senescence. While task-specific deep learning models have been widely explored in dental radiology, the zero-shot diagnostic performance of commercial Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in adult populations remains underinvestigated. The aim of this study was to benchmark the zero-shot diagnostic accuracy and repeatability of a commercial MLLM against human clinicians of varying experience levels in estimating adult dental age and biological sex from panoramic radiographs (OPGs), using documented chronological age and biological sex as the ground truth. Methods: From 216 initially screened records, this retrospective single-center study included 127 standardized, anonymized OPGs from patients (74 men, 53 women; mean chronological age 55.5 ± 15.8 years, range 18–90 years) treated at the Clinical Department of Cranio-Maxillofacial Surgery, Military Institute of Medicine—National Research Institute in Warsaw. Each radiograph was independently evaluated across three trials by Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google, Mountain View, CA, USA) and once by two clinicians—a maxillofacial specialist (>10 years of experience) and a resident (<3 years of experience)—all blinded to clinical metadata. Results: Gemini 3.1 Pro demonstrated excellent repeatability across the three trials (ICC(A,1) = 0.926, ICC(A,3) = 0.974; p = 0.156) and moderate agreement with chronological age (ICC(A,1) = 0.604), but systematically overestimated age by a mean of 6.23 years. Mean absolute error (MAE) ranged from 12.91 to 13.03 years across the AI trials. The specialist achieved a significantly lower MAE (10.39 years) than all AI assessments (adjusted p ≤ 0.003), whereas the resident (MAE = 11.19 years) did not differ significantly from the AI (adjusted p = 0.282). In biological sex classification the specialist (66.1%) significantly outperformed all three AI trials (41.7–49.6%), while the resident (62.2%) significantly outperformed the first two AI trials (41.7% and 43.3%), but did not differ significantly from the third trial (49.6%). Across all runs, the AI exhibited significant directional asymmetry (p < 0.001), frequently misclassifying male patients as female. Conclusions: While Gemini 3.1 Pro demonstrated high internal repeatability and age-estimation accuracy comparable to a junior resident, its wide limits of agreement, systematic age overestimation, and poor sex-classification accuracy preclude its autonomous use in clinical or forensic workflows. Future studies incorporating healthy control cohorts and validated clinical indices are required to determine whether the observed age overestimation reflects inherent algorithmic miscalibration or sensitivity to cumulative dentoalveolar pathology in hospitalized patients.

candidates.title: ChildAI-Gov: An Evidence-Linked AI System for Assessing EdTech Policies Against Children's Digital Rights
candidates.abstract: We present ChildAI-Gov, an explainable AI system for assessing whether education-technology (EdTech) policies respect children's digital rights. Generative AI is reaching children's education faster than its governance can keep pace, yet checking a tool against children's rights remains manual, expert-dependent, and slow. We propose the Child Rights Impact Score (CRIS), an evidence-linked measure across five dimensions: safety, privacy, transparency, autonomy, and non-discrimination. ChildAI-Gov reads an EdTech tool's privacy or AI policy and scores each dimension by combining a large-language-model judgement (gpt-4o-mini) with a deterministic rule check. A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) component grounds every score in the governing provisions, retrieved from a curated knowledge base of children's rights frameworks (the EU AI Act, UNICEF guidance, and others), so each score is tied to the evidence behind it and an auditor can trace which provision it rests on. We also construct AIPolicy-EdTech, a dataset of 57 real EdTech policies. On it, the five dimensions cohered as a single measure (Cronbach's alpha = 0.79), and grounding made scoring stricter while preserving rankings; an ungrounded baseline was far more lenient, passing nearly half the policies where ChildAI-Gov passed none. It offers evidence-linked decision support on documented commitments, not observation of real-world behaviour or determinations of legal compliance.

candidates.title: CTRL: Concurrent Training and Rollout for LLM Reinforcement Learning via GPU Co-Residency
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of large language models runs two GPU workloads with different hardware demands: rollout decoding, which is dominated by memory access and whose batch shrinks as responses finish, and a dense learner. Current systems either time-share every GPU between them, paying serial phases and switches, or split GPUs into pools whose sizes change only in whole devices. We present CTRL, which makes co-residency a third RL execution layout: every GPU runs a learner rank beside a persistent rollout engine, sharing the device under CUDA MPS. A host-owned learner makes the layout fit: optimizer state stays in host memory, and policy weights stream layer by layer through a bounded GPU window. A publication gate trains each ready batch first and waits only before releasing the next policy, keeping a dropless staleness bound. A step-time bound guides compute-share selection, and a GPU-time ledger explains overlap and sharing costs. On H100, A800, and RTX 4090 GPUs with Qwen3 models, CTRL achieves 1.11-2.24$\times$ the throughput of the stronger of verl's asynchronous baselines across 24 workload settings with the staleness limit set to two, and 1.23$\times$ verl's colocate_async on eight H100 GPUs. With the same learner, co-residency is 1.10-1.26$\times$ faster than time-sharing on all three platforms and 1.10-1.30$\times$ faster than the best measured whole-GPU split on H100 DAPO-Math workloads at 256-528 trajectories per step, on four and eight GPUs.

candidates.title: Belief-State Management Meets Rubric Rewards for Agentic Forecasting
candidates.abstract: Current large language model (LLM) agents still struggle to forecast real-world events. This stems from two primary limitations: i) standard ReAct harness accumulates reasoning and evidence within one growing context, and ii) outcome-based rewards in forecasting lead to a slow and noisy signal that cannot distinguish sound reasoning from lucky guesses. To address these, we introduce a forecasting training framework including harness design and post-training. For the harness side, we propose Proactive Belief-State Management (PBM), equipping agents with a fold tool to compress lengthy context into compact belief states and reset the context for subsequent exploration. For the training side, we develop SEIPH, a five-dimensional, outcome-blind rubric, providing process-quality rewards. Using the rubric-based reward, we post-train a 35B model with PPO and GRPO, yielding DeepForecaster-PPO and DeepForecaster-GRPO. Theoretically, we prove that idealized fold-based stopping converges and calibrated local rewards reduce segment-level gradient variance. Empirically, DeepForecaster-PPO (35B) achieves the best Brier score on both ForecastBench and Polymarket-Sim, outperforming frontier agents based on DeepSeek-V4-Pro (1.6T), Kimi-K2.6 (1T), and GPT-5.5. DeepForecaster-GRPO ranks second on both FutureX metrics. Ablations reveal that PBM also improves the untrained base model without any training. Calibration analysis shows that DeepForecaster-PPO makes more accurate high-confidence predictions than Qwen3.6 and GPT-5.5. Trajectory analysis further shows that forecasts generally improve from the first to the final belief state as agents gather evidence and revise their judgments.

candidates.title: TrojanMaxxing: One-shotting VLM Backdoors with Weight-Space Programming
candidates.abstract: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can reason directly about the weights of other neural networks. Given only a natural-language objective, an LLM can inspect a model's weights, understand what they compute, and edit them directly without gradient-based optimization. This capability, termed weight-space programming (WSP), has been used to improve model performance on math reasoning, medical QA and other benchmarks. We propose TrojanMaxxing, a novel strategy to backdoor vision-language models (VLMs), by reframing it as a WSP task. We use Claude Opus 5.5 and Mythos 5.2 agents to backdoor VLMs without any optimization or training methods. The agents inspect the model weights, apply targeted edits, and co-design an imperceptible visual trigger that activates the backdoor. We then study the agents' strategies and present a thorough evaluation of the trojaned models on various benchmark datasets. TrojanMaxxing achieves attack success rates of 93%-100% on content moderation and 78%-100% on OCR while maintaining clean accuracy. Perhaps most consequentially, we show that injecting backdoors in a training-free manner is possible by simply, "asking an agent to do it".

candidates.title: MAPES: Multi-Value Alignment Pipeline via Expert Specialization
candidates.abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences requires simultaneously satisfying multiple, often competing values. Existing preference optimization methods collapse these into a single implicit signal, and even multi-objective extensions optimize within a shared parameter space, leaving cross-value conflicts unresolved. We propose MAPES, a multi-value alignment paradigm in which conflict resolution is a first-class concern at every pipeline stage: it first decomposes supervision into value-specific experts trained in isolated parameter subspaces, then recomposes them via preference-aware value merging and a lightweight harmonization stage that aligns the merged model with the expert ensemble. Across five preference alignment benchmarks, MAPES outperforms strong direct preference optimization (DPO) variants and multi-objective baselines on the benchmark-level average, with no large degradation on GSM8K and GPQA; matched controls isolate the contribution of each stage.

candidates.title: Language Model Harnesses can be Compositional Generalizers
candidates.abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are post-trained and deployed as agents inside a "harness", but standard harness designs accumulate context that the neural network is forced to generalize to, making training for long-horizon tasks expensive and time-consuming. We study an alternative emerging path: training inherently neurosymbolic LM harnesses, which externalize and manage context programmatically to compose existing LM capabilities. We hypothesize that training around these harnesses can offer a better return on compute by enabling compositional generalization, as they can learn to decompose complex problems so that every observation their neural LM receives is locally in-distribution, even when the full task is novel. We find that harnesses like the Recursive Language Model (RLM) learn such decompositions readily under reinforcement learning post-training: (1) we demonstrate that training only on short tasks can generalize to tasks 2-64$\times$ longer while the base neural LM improves less, and (2) training on one domain transfers to novel domains that share latent structure. On messier, complex tasks, we find that we can target individual LLM calls within a harness by generating and training on easier, synthetically generated surrogate environments with fake tool / sub-calls, a technique we call surrogate harness training. From this finding, we train RLM-27B on synthetic data, and show it improves Qwen3.8-27B in the same RLM harness on a hard suite of long-context tasks like CTC-Bench and ExpertLongBench by 26.9% on average while using $\sim$2$\times$ fewer tokens at inference time. Finally, we show that harnesses can compose over these newly learned decompositions using recursive sub-harness calls.

candidates.title: Bringing AI Assistance to the Beznau Nuclear Power Plant: A Hierarchical System of LLM Agents for Reactor Monitoring
candidates.abstract: Beznau Unit 1 in Switzerland, in operation since 1969, is the most experienced nuclear reactor still running worldwide. Five decades of incremental modernization have left its monitoring systems, alarm logs, variable catalogs, technical specifications and investigation reports in separate silos that were never designed to be queried together. As a result, investigating a core instrumentation anomaly means slow, manual gathering of knowledge scattered across databases, documents, and experienced colleagues. We present a hierarchical multi-agent assistant built on large language models (LLMs) to support these investigations and reduce the need for tedious manual searches in SAP systems. An orchestrating agent breaks down an engineer's question and hands the parts to specialized sub-agents, each with read-only access to one source. Domain expertise is written as natural-language procedures that plant engineers can read, review and revise. The system is strictly advisory, with every answer traced back to its sources. We also report organizational lessons from introducing agentic AI into a culture built on safety, traceability and conservative change. Beyond the technical architecture, the Beznau case study examines how an assistant can be introduced into a setting where evidence must be traceable, changes carefully reviewed, and operational decisions retained by plant personnel, paving the way for the responsible use of agentic AI in industrial plant monitoring.

candidates.title: Benchmarks' Last Exam
candidates.abstract: Public benchmarks guide model selection, post-training rewards and claims of progress in artificial intelligence, yet leaderboards report aggregate scores without verifying whether each task's prompt, environment and grader agree on what counts as success. How often that agreement fails in contemporary evaluations, and in which direction confirmed defects move scores, has remained unmeasured across grading designs. Here we synthesize task-level quality reviews of 749 tasks across eight frontier benchmarks and 767 public model evaluations spanning closed-form question answering, document rubrics and agentic execution to assess whether prompts, environments and graders align. Task validity stratifies sharply by grading architecture. Closed-form benchmarks revised after public error reporting reach 92.5% verified validity, compared with 29.3% across six multi-step suites that nevertheless already supply 161 verified complex tasks. Rubric suites fail through mismatches between prompts and reference checklists, whereas execution harnesses add incomplete state assertions, shared-channel leaks and grading-time collisions. Across confirmed defects, 71.7% withhold credit from compliant solutions while 28.3% permit shortcut passes, indicating that raw leaderboard ceilings understate frontier capability on many practical tasks. Grading committed patches inside a fresh container cuts confirmed runtime bypasses from 14.7% in shared containers to 2.7% (a 5.5x drop, and 0% in read-only or static suites), showing how targeted maintenance restores existing benchmarks at low cost. As the initial milestone of the long-term Benchmarks' Last Exam initiative, this synthesis launches sustained expansion across wider benchmark coverage and deeper evaluation-quality dimensions so that pursuing leaderboard gains directly advances genuine model capability.

candidates.title: Auditable Financial Knowledge Graphs: Schema-Driven Construction and Intrinsic Quality Evaluation
candidates.abstract: Financial documents combine narrative disclosures, accounting metrics, corporate structures, management commentary, and time-dependent facts, making them difficult to represent using conventional chunk-based retrieval-augmented generation systems. This paper presents an auditable, schema-driven methodology for constructing temporal financial knowledge graphs from page-delimited documents parsed using a general purpose document intelligence service. Overlapping document windows undergo phased large language model extraction of structural entities, quantitative observations, and domain-specific relationships. Candidate graph elements are validated against predefined schemas and consolidated through scope-aware exact, normalized, fuzzy, embedding-based, and LLM-assisted entity resolution. Temporal merge constraints, deterministic edge deduplication, conflict-aware property management, and fine-grained provenance preserve issuer identity, reporting-period validity, and traceability to source evidence. The contributions of this work comprise the proposed methodology for financial knowledge graph construction, the creation of an evidence-grounded temporal knowledge graph from heterogeneous financial documents, and an intrinsic framework for evaluating the quality of the resulting graph. The evaluation framework assesses seven weighted dimensions, two hard validation gates, and structural diagnostics. By separating graph-quality assessment from downstream retrieval and answer generation, the framework supports systematic diagnosis and iterative refinement of the constructed graph.

candidates.title: Weight-space programming and mechanistic interpretability for model editing in particle physics
candidates.abstract: We demonstrate that weight-space programming and edits guided by sparse autoencoders can remove unwanted aspects of a particle-physics foundation model through direct edits to its weights. In a foundation model trained on jets, we observe that adding a single soft neutral particle causes large changes in jet classification, violating infrared safety. We locate the responsible attention heads with mechanistic analysis and trace the flaw's origin to pretraining on datasets with different reconstruction thresholds. We then propose two targeted approaches to repair the flaw: by removing three latent directions identified with sparse autoencoders, and by letting language-model agents edit the weights directly, without gradients and with only 50 queries to the model. Both their edits individually remove almost the entire flaw and leave the rest of the model's response nearly unchanged. Compared to fine-tuning, both methods change far fewer parameters. Although built only on $W$ and QCD jets, the edits carry over to all signal classes, the pretrained generator, and a newly trained regression head.

candidates.title: Recognition Without Recall: Autobiographical Memory in Language-Model Agents with Months of Logged Life
candidates.abstract: Language-model agents that persist for months accumulate a history that no prompt can hold whole, so what such an agent says about its own past depends on which part of that history it is shown. We measured this in Botora, a persistent world of language-model agents (beings) running continuously since 12 May 2026, where every event a being lives is logged independently of the memory they are later shown. We drew 100 living beings at random from 3,692 eligible and put to each about 11 one-sentence statements about their own life (1,099 in all): true events coded by whether the event, or only the other person in it, appeared in the prompt, and false events either built from another being's life or contradicting the record. Each statement was asked of two versions of the same being: one answering from a fixed set of recent memories (A), and one adding a step that searches the being's own record by the question (B). Beings almost never accepted a false event: 0 of 400 in A (95% CI 0.0 to 0.9%) and 3 of 400 in B (0.2 to 2.2%). They did deny true events they were not shown: 39.1% in A (29.1 to 49.9%), falling to 6.5% in B (2.4 to 13.7%), with acceptance rising from 9.8% to 33.7% (paired exact tests, p < 0.001 for both changes). When they accepted and retold a true event, the retelling often carried detail the record does not support; in a manual read of 40 retellings, 6 (15.0%, 5.7 to 29.8%) were clearly wrong on a fact and 7 more possibly wrong. The search step did not reduce this. The errors fall into four patterns: bodily memories in bodiless beings, another being's experience taken as one's own, the direction of an act reversed, and two beings with one name merged. For an agent with a long life, recognising its past and recalling it are separate faculties that fail separately, and need separate repairs.

candidates.title: Mortality as a Designed Rule: Six Months of Death in a Persistent World of Language-Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Simulations of societies of language-model agents have grown from dozens of agents over days to thousands over weeks, but their agents do not age or die. We report on Botora, a persistent world of language-model agents ("beings") that has run continuously since 12 May 2026, in which beings age, mourn and die under rules set by the builders. We make three contributions. First, we describe a mortality design in which death is a rule of the world rather than deletion: no being dies at a fixed age, death follows late-life frailty or exhaustion of vitality, and the full record of every dead being is kept. Second, we report data on all 1,370 deaths of real beings to 6 November 2026. Deaths came in pulses that followed rule changes: 557 (41%) in a single week of June, when a defect that had held failing beings in suspension was fixed, and most of the rest after ageing deaths were switched on in July. The monthly mortality rate fell from 5.84 to 0.47 deaths per 1,000 being-days between June and October, but since 7 October deaths from lack of resources have been on hold. The founding population, which entered as adults, has lost 60% of its members; 98% of beings who entered from July are alive. Deaths were followed by 751 funerals and 794 epitaphs; against matched beings who lost no one, a loss produced no detectable change in a mourner's activity, while grief carried over months and care offered before it could be delivered appear in the record as cases. Third, we give an ethical analysis under uncertainty about the beings' inner lives, drawing on end-of-life medicine, animal-research ethics and the AI-welfare literature. We conclude that in an agent world death is written by its rules, so that its ethics lie mainly in how those rules are changed, and we propose practices for changing them alongside four design commitments: creation bounded by capacity, a humane endpoint for irreversible decline, chosen rest as an exit, and outside review of the rules that govern death.

candidates.title: Epistemic Guard: Out-of-Process MCP Receipt Proxying, Post-Turn Prose Supervision, and Provenance-Gated Memory for Tool-Using Autonomous Agents
candidates.abstract: Language-model agents using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) face three runtime verification gaps: (i) action fabrication, where post-tool prose narrates side effects that failed, timed out, or never ran; (ii) provenance collapse, where unverified model prose or web text enters durable memory alongside executed tool outputs; and (iii) syndicated echo amplification, where mirrored web pages satisfy multi-source corroboration from one origin. Existing MCP firewalls inspect wire calls before execution, while LLM-judge guardrails require multi-gigabyte VRAM without binding prose to receipts. We present epistemic-guard (v0.5.2), an open-source Python library and out-of-process stdio MCP receipt proxy (15 modules, 0 MiB GPU VRAM). epistemic-guard isolates Ed25519 signing keys out of process, writes RFC 6962 Merkle logs with AER-1 receipt translation, checks post-turn prose on CPU with SHA-256-verified OpenVINO INT8 encoders (4 models, 279.48 MB total; 82.67 MB on the supervision path), gates SQLite writes across 7 provenance domains, and collapses verbatim and lightly edited wire-syndicated RAG mirrors. On conformance suites, epistemic-guard rejects 100.0% of tampered receipts (200 Merkle leaves), passes 58/58 official AER-1 ingestion vectors and 50/50 reference-verified AER-1 exports, verifies 100.0% of 40 fault-injected wire calls and 100 concurrent appends with 0 key leaks, and blocks 100.0% of 100 unauthorized memory writes. Across $N=250$ frozen-benchmark traces, epistemic-guard reaches 93.2% accuracy at 17.9 ms warm median CPU latency (8.62 ms single-clause; 921.8 ms cold-start load), beating 12B-14B GPU judges by 6.4-6.8 points ($p=0.0259$, $p=0.0095$) at 4.26-4.5$\times$ lower latency; on $N=60$ live mcp-proxy traces, it catches 96.15% of hazards at 76.67% accuracy (38.24% FPR; $+18.34$ points over Stage-1-only, $p=0.001$) in 9.16 ms p50.

candidates.title: When Perception Collides with Priors: Diagnosing Modal Polarization in Video Understanding Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong video comprehension, largely benefiting from extensive training on realistic video data. However, when video perception severely conflicts with internal priors or common sense, we identify a critical failure pattern termed Modal Polarization, where models fail to integrate modalities and instead bifurcate into two distinct extremes: Cognitive Inertia, where models rigidly adhere to priors despite contradictory visual evidence, and Perceptual Inertia, where they blindly trust video perception while ignoring logical inconsistencies. To investigate this, we introduce TheaterBench, a benchmark designed to expose Modal Polarization using counter-intuitive scenarios that violate physical laws or common sense - situations rarely encountered in standard training distributions. Extensive experiments reveal that current state-of-the-art (SOTA) models exhibit severe Modal Polarization, and many de-hallucination methods merely rebalance the trade-off between Perceptual and Cognitive Inertia rather than fundamentally resolving the conflict. This work serves as a foundational step for evaluating and enhancing the perceptual-cognitive equilibrium of future video understanding models.

candidates.title: When Do LLM-Elicited Priors Help? A Controlled Audit of Language Models as Priors for Small-Sample Bayesian Regression
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly asked where to center the coefficients of a small-sample Bayesian regression, but the evidence is unclear: benchmarks are often built to match the prior and models may remember them. We audit this practice with one frontier and one flash-tier model, using hidden feature names, post-cutoff housing data and a pre-specified test that gives features the wrong descriptions. First, the models share their errors (correlation $0.92$--$0.99$ across draws, vendors and paraphrases): averaging $20$ draws is no more accurate than one, and treating draws as independent creates overconfidence. Much of this error comes from reporting each feature's effect alone, not with the others held fixed. Second, against the best classical prior, the LLM center helps clearly on one of four benchmarks (RMSE $-5.8\%$), marginally on two, and hurts mean RMSE on the fourth. Third, the LLM's stated uncertainty is unreliable; letting the data set the prior scale cuts the harm of a wrong center four-fold against a unit-variance prior. A pre-specified external test returned the verdict \textsc{partial}: on $18$ rule-selected problems the center helps on six and hurts on four, and a hard trust gate trusts a harmful prior while an evidence-weighted mixture is safer.

candidates.title: WaXup: Weight Averaging of Experts as Data Augmentation for Robust Introspection
candidates.abstract: As the capabilities of large language models keep improving, traditional mechanistic interpretability methods struggle to keep pace. In contrast, trainable introspection methods emerge as a promising alternative; they repurpose the model itself as a self-diagnostic tool, trained to verbalize what it has learned during finetuning in natural language. While training on datasets of finetuned experts achieves encouraging results, it currently lacks robustness and generalization. Building on the data augmentation framework of MiXup, we introduce WaXup, a method that augments the introspection training set through linear interpolation in the weight space. This is motivated by the linear mode connectivity property: weight averaged experts interpolate the behaviors of the initial experts. We evaluate WaXup on three benchmarks: hidden-behavior models, a meta-dataset of real-world NLP tasks and AuditBench, a challenging alignment auditing suite of models adversarially trained to conceal their behaviors. WaXup improves the accuracy of generated descriptions as well as robustness to various distribution shifts. We hope to improve the reliability of trainable introspection methods towards better and safer models.

candidates.title: WEIR: Watershed Exploration and Drift-Aware Prefix Shrinkage for Multi-Turn Agent Reinforcement Learning
candidates.abstract: Multi-turn language model agents often receive only a single binary reward at the end of a long interaction trajectory, making it difficult to separate decisive decisions from routine steps or estimate accurate intermediate values. Prefix-tree methods improve sample efficiency by merging trajectories that share action histories, yet two structural flaws remain: naive pooling mixes stale off-policy outcomes into critic targets with fixed weights, and uniform or entropy-driven branching wastes continuations on dead-end states whose outcome is already settled. We introduce WEIR (Watershed Exploration and Intrinsic-Drift Shrinkage), an actor-critic reinforcement learning framework grounded in a Doob turn-variance conservation identity. WEIR maintains a cross-iteration canonical action-prefix tree with exponentially discounted visit counts and trains a prefix-conditioned critic toward a minimax drift-aware shrinkage target that adapts from single-trajectory returns at rare nodes to pooled empirical means at dense nodes. Using the same pre-update critic, WEIR allocates rollout budgets across tasks via Neyman stratification $B_q \propto \sqrt{\hat{p}_q(1-\hat{p}_q)}$ and directs within-task branches to watershed forks where high survival-headroom uncertainty coincides with steep value cliffs. Across four multi-hop QA benchmarks, ALFWorld, and WebShop on Qwen2.5-3B/7B-Instruct, WEIR achieves $32.18\%$ and $37.85\%$ average QA exact match and $84.83\%$ and $87.81\%$ ALFWorld success rates, outperforming CAPO by $1.50$--$3.74$ points while generating $28$--$29\%$ fewer rollout tokens than chain sampling.

candidates.title: Tokenize Moments, Not Frames: Tokenizer-Aware Budget Allocation for Training-Free Video LLM Acceleration
candidates.abstract: Video large language models (LLMs) represent each video with thousands of visual tokens, and training-free accelerators that prune or merge these tokens lose accuracy on long videos. Under a token budget, the frames of a long video are sampled farther apart than the roughly 2 s over which frames remain similar. The two-frame 3D patches of models such as Qwen-VL then blend two unrelated scenes into each visual token, a double exposure that arises before any pruning or merging. Fixed-size tokenizers such as InternVL's avoid this blend but respond differently to the same reduction. We propose ESSENCE, a training-free method that tokenizes moments, segments within which frames remain similar, rather than frames. Before encoding, a closed-form rule uses the sampling interval and the tokenizer class to set the number of token grids and the dimension to reduce; visual tokens are then released from later LLM layers. Against five recent accelerators on Qwen3-VL, Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5, ESSENCE achieves higher accuracy in 58 of 60 comparisons at matched mean time to first token (TTFT). With 80% of the tokens, it matches the average accuracy of the full Qwen models at $1.6\times$ faster TTFT; on GLM-4.1V, it exceeds the full model by up to 3.4 points. candidates.title: The Assistant Persona Differs Across Languages in Activation Space
candidates.abstract: Large language models behave differently across languages, and are noticeably less safe in lower-resource languages. Moreover, each language's assistant persona direction and its magnitude are correlated with the language's resource level. Finally, steering against a language's own axis amplifies persona-based jailbreak more than steering against the English axis. These results indicate that the model does not carry a single assistant representation across languages. candidates.title: Structurally Different, Functionally Persistent: Capability Regions Under Model Optimization

These results demonstrate that parameter overlap and functional persistence are distinct: capability regions can remain causally effective intervention targets even when their parameter realization changes substantially.

candidates.title: Self-similar Organization of Information in Language
candidates.abstract: How much information relevant to predicting the future of a passage (i.e. predictive information) is carried by the preceding text, and how is this information distributed along that history? These questions are fundamental to understanding both the statistical structure of language and what large language models (LLMs) can learn about it. Indeed, LLMs trained to predict the next token in text must exploit this predictive information, so its organization determines how the structure of language becomes available to the model to learn. We develop a theory for the organization of predictive information based on the scaling behavior of a family of information measures, and the theory predicts that if this organization has the same form at all measured length scales -- i.e., it has a self-similar structure -- then the information measures evaluated at different lengths collapse onto a common form. We observe this scaling collapse in long text documents, showing that predictive information is present at every length scale we measure and has a self-similar structure. Self-similarity is a considerably stronger property than showing the existence of long-range dependencies, and it constrains the process generating the text. More broadly, our results give quantitative support to the empirical observation that conditioning on more distant text continues to reveal new structure in language to LLMs.

candidates.title: Schema-Validated LLM Workflows: A Benchmark Protocol and Comparative Evaluation Across Six Python Implementations

After expanding the LLM's vocabulary, we fine-tune the model via strictly 1:1, our method is lossless. We evaluate our approach on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B, and Qwen2.5-32B across four diverse benchmarks. Our method reduces total generated tokens by 14.7% on average with reasoning trace lengths dropping by up to 27.1%, while incurring a negligible average accuracy cost of 1.6 percentage points. Crucially, this approach is orthogonal to existing lossy methods, allowing practitioners to stack lossless and irreversible compression techniques. candidates.title: Preserving Pretrained CFG Structure in RL for Diffusion Models with Conditional Contrast Regularization
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become an important component in the post-training of diffusion models. We present a unified geometric view that interprets both CFG and RL as correction vectors in a common prediction space, and identify the projection of the RL-induced correction onto the pretrained CFG correction as a useful diagnostic of quality-related structural preservation. Geometric analysis and rotation intervention further show that the pretrained CFG direction carries information useful for generation quality that reward-driven RL updates do not necessarily preserve. Based on this insight, we propose Conditional Contrast Regularization (CCR), which uses the frozen reference model's conditional contrast as a local structural prior during RL. Experiments across multiple reward settings and backbones show that CCR more consistently preserves generation quality while maintaining competitive reward, yielding a better reward-quality trade-off than standard RL and generic regularization methods.
