candidates.title: Large language models as oncology world models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can synthesize cancer patient cases, but their internal representation of oncology, or world model, has not been explored systematically. By only specifying tumor type, we show that LLMs tend to generate similar patients per cancer, with on average 81.0% to 93.2% of a cancer's patients sharing the most frequent value of each baseline feature. By systematically varying patient features in 12 clinical scenarios, we show that they follow biomarker and treatment logic in 29 of 36 model-scenario assessments, against 1 of 12 when previous treatment or frailty matters. Continuing real patient trajectories, an LLM predicted 89.9% 12-month survival, and 79.2% with similar patients as examples, against 72.2% observed. To represent these trajectories, we developed the Clinical State Space, a dynamic representation framework that we also applied to real patients. Despite the limits we show, improved world models may support digital twins, which our framework can evaluate.

candidates.title: Do Large Language Models Understand Financial Fraud?
candidates.abstract: Banks and compliance teams are exploring large language models (LLMs) as fraud analysts. Money laundering, however, is a structural crime. A single laundering transaction looks ordinary, and the evidence lies in how funds move across accounts. An LLM can only support anti-money-laundering (AML) work if it uses this structure rather than surface features. We test whether current LLMs do. We evaluate Claude, GPT-4.1, Phi-4, and Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite on 6,302 transactions from the IBM AML dataset. The benchmark keeps all 370 labeled laundering instances whole across eight typologies. We vary the context from a single transaction, to transaction history, to history with typology definitions and chain-of-thought reasoning. Only two of the four models beat chance, and only with the richest context. Their recall follows how often an account repeats within a laundering instance, not the shape of the instance. They detect hub-based typologies such as fan-in far better than bipartite or cycle typologies. The four models also rarely agree on which transactions are suspicious. These results suggest that current LLMs use repeated account activity as a proxy for fraud, and that they are not yet ready to serve as standalone AML detectors.

candidates.title: Comparison of Multimodal Large Language Models for Phytoplankton Identification from Microscopy Images
candidates.abstract: Phytoplankton composition and biomass are widely used indicators of eutrophication and aquatic ecosystem condition. Under the EU Water Framework Directive, phytoplankton is a biological quality element in ecological status assessment, which requires reliable taxonomic identification. This study evaluated the capabilities and limitations of general-purpose multimodal AI for phytoplankton identification from microscopy images using a two-stage design. In Stage 1, six off-the-shelf multimodal models—ChatGPT 5.1, ChatGPT 5.4, Gemini 3 Thinking, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Perplexity Pro and Grok 4.1—were compared using 30 expert-verified microscopy image cases. Gemini 3 Thinking showed the strongest overall performance across several measures, although no stable model hierarchy was established across all metrics. In Stage 2, GPT-5.6 Sol was evaluated using an expanded dataset of 157 microscopy images in three independent runs. Accuracy ranged from 70.1 to 81.5% at the higher-group level and from 40.1 to 57.3% at the genus level, but decreased to 14.3–31.8% at the species level. Performance differed significantly among runs and phytoplankton groups, with recurrent taxon-specific misclassification patterns. Across both stages, performance declined markedly with increasing taxonomic resolution. General-purpose multimodal AI may therefore support preliminary phytoplankton image screening and broad-group assignment, but current systems remain insufficiently reliable for autonomous genus- or species-level identification. Expert verification remains essential for ecological monitoring and water quality assessment.

candidates.title: Challenges of Single-Reference Benchmarks for Clinical Reasoning in Large Language Model–Based Decision Support
candidates.abstract: Unlabelled: This viewpoint addresses developers and evaluators of large language model (LLM)-based clinical decision support systems. Although recent benchmarks increasingly evaluate multiple clinical reasoning domains, many still rely substantially on reference decision agreement-whether model outputs conform to predefined decisions. Our aim is to clarify when such agreement remains useful, when it becomes insufficient for complex or preference-sensitive decisions, and how it can be complemented by reasoning-centered assessment. Clinical decision-making often depends on structured reasoning under uncertainty, integrating probabilistic evidence, contextual constraints, and patient values. Using oncology as an illustrative domain, we argue that some decision variability is a structural feature of clinical reasoning rather than noise or error. Used alone in such settings, single-reference benchmarks may conflate reasonable divergence with incorrectness and reward answer imitation over transparent reasoning. We conclude that reference decision agreement should be retained for tasks with stable ground truth but supplemented by evidence grounding, reasoning quality, patient-centeredness, and safety checks for open-ended clinical decision support. This multidimensional approach is intended to support safer and more clinically meaningful evaluation.

candidates.title: Adaptive Retrieval and Evidence Calibration for Reliable Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can expose a response to incorrect evidence when a retrieved source is plausible but mismatched. This paper presents ACRE, a compact pipeline that couples query-dependent reranking depth, source-evidence confidence estimation, and a selective output decision. A BM25 candidate list is augmented with lexical similarity signals; logistic confidence models select one, three, or five candidates and determine whether a verbatim, source-attributed answer should be issued. We evaluate on 300 authentic news reports and 50 out-of-index reports from the Lee text corpora, using 1,400 reproducibly derived source-identification queries. On the 280-query held-out split, adaptive retrieval matches the BM25 top-1 source accuracy of 77.86% while requiring only 1.73 candidates per query in the assigned reranking depth, versus five for the fixed-depth alternative. With the development-selected abstention threshold, the system responds to 80.36% of test queries at 91.11% accepted-source accuracy; its expected calibration error is 0.039. The results demonstrate an economical approach to coupling retrieval efficiency with calibrated source attribution in an explicitly extractive RAG setting.

candidates.title: Vision-Language-Action Models: A Life-Cycle Survey of Design, Training and Deployment
candidates.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt web-pretrained vision-language models to output robot actions, so that web knowledge carries over to physical control. In under four years the field has grown from RT-2, the first VLA, to open models that fine-tune on a single consumer GPU and proprietary generalists that clean unseen homes. VLA research joins robotics, computer vision and language modelling, so this survey is written for researchers and practitioners from each of these fields. It reviews 89 works from December 2022 to October 2026, mainly on manipulation and navigation, plus humanoid control, world-action models and evaluation. Seven design axes follow a VLA's life cycle: model design (inputs and memory, architecture, action output, intermediate predictions), training (pretraining data, post-training) and deployment (real-time execution). We compare 22 models on these axes, with their training data, model size, inference speed and hardware. Three trends emerge. (i) Training data has broadened beyond teleoperated robot data (about 10,000 hours for $π_0$) to community-collected episodes and egocentric human video (20,000 hours for GR00T N1.7). (ii) Model sizes have split into two groups: most recent models have 3-7 billion parameters; a new group under one billion runs on consumer GPUs. (iii) Generalist VLAs handling both manipulation and navigation are emerging, such as UniVLA and Qwen-VLA. We also compare VLAs with world-action models, which predict future observations as well as actions, and review evidence that some VLAs with near-perfect benchmark scores fail after small scene changes. A practitioner's guide gives a default for each design decision, and a glossary supports readers new to the field.

candidates.title: Query-Aware Context Compression for Efficient Long-Context Language Model Inference
candidates.abstract: Query-aware context compression can reduce the amount of source text forwarded to a language model, but keyword ranking may discard evidence connected through intermediate entities. We present QAB-R, a training-free sentence selector combining BM25, query-identifier-constrained anchor selection, canonicalized entity matching, and at most two bridge-linked candidates under a fixed sentence budget. We first evaluate a single-bridge baseline on 300 synthetic single- and two-hop queries. We then execute 300 additional held-out stress cases covering paraphrases, competing entity notes, identifier formatting variation, and combined changes; a separate 60-case test extends source contexts to 58,368 whitespace-delimited words. At a 10% sentence budget, QAB-R preserved complete two-hop support in all 60 cases of each stress condition, whereas single-bridge retention fell to 0% under competing notes and format changes. For 1,024 fact pairs, the median QAB-R CPU preprocessing time was 66.3 ms, and the selected text contained 5,741 of 58,368 input words. The study reports evidence completeness, retained input length, and CPU preprocessing cost; downstream reader accuracy and GPU inference speed are distinct system-level outcomes.

candidates.title: Ontology-Guided, Verifiable In-Silico Experiments on Lumped-Parameter Cardiovascular Models: Semantic Connection Checking, SHACL Validation and a Receipt-Verified Language-Model Agent
candidates.abstract: Composing physiological models from independent components fails at the joints: same-unit variables can carry different meanings, metadata can be correct while the attached numbers are wrong, and a language model that writes the report can state results never computed. We present an open framework treating each separately. The core is a deterministic six-compartment closed-loop cardiovascular model integrated as a hybrid system of valve regimes with runtime conservation, positivity, valve and settling audits. A semantic layer annotates 34 variables with label-checked Ontology of Physics for Biology properties and Uberon/FMA anatomy, exports named-graph RDF and provides a fail-closed connection validator requiring agreement of property, anatomy, bearer, reference, temporal context and flow orientation before a value is transferred. In a 12-fixture fault-injection benchmark it rejects eight of nine unsafe connections an unguarded baseline accepts; its retained blind spot, correct left-ventricular metadata on right-ventricular data, passes with errors up to 129.8 mmHg. An evidence-first review of the Smith et al. (2004) CellML model produced a variable dictionary, anatomical node specification, SHACL shapes and PROV-O records; on the model’s published SemSim annotation they report 22 violations, 7 warnings and 46 informational results. A tool-calling language-model agent plans baseline-versus-intervention experiments under a three-layer scope guard; it chooses only runs and metric paths, and every sentence and number in its report is written by code from tool receipts and re-verified. In a 27-case evaluation three providers passed every case; all 14 out-of-scope clinical requests were refused before any model call. Nothing is clinically validated; parameters are exploratory, claim boundaries stated. Code, evidence (redacted where required), shapes, provenance and traces are public.

candidates.title: Superfluid: Local AI Server for Distributed LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Running large language models (LLMs) on local devices keeps data private, removes per-token cost, cuts network latency, and keeps working without a connection. Two shifts now strain how such models are served. On one device, several agents share a locally served model with an interactive user. Across devices, a developer or small team often owns several capable machines from different vendors, which sit idle most of the day because every local server serves one runtime on one machine. We present Superfluid, an open-source LLM server built for local inference at both scales. On one device, Superfluid drives llama.cpp, MLX, or BaseRT in isolated worker processes through one scheduler that moves interactive requests ahead of agent work, computes a prompt shared by many requests once, and writes every token to a durable log before it reaches the client. Across devices, one Superfluid server turns a fleet of machines into a single API endpoint. Machines with different hardware serve copies of the same model, receive work according to their measured speed, and can join or fail under load without losing a request. For Qwen3.8-27B on an Apple M5 Pro, a chat sent while eight agents are working receives its first token in 1.5 s, against 291-612 s on llama-server, Ollama, and mlx_lm.server. On six machines from three chip vendors serving 64 simulated users for one hour, Superfluid answers all 5,041 requests while machines join one at a time and one is killed and rejoins; throughput grows from 112 to 534 tok/s and the median first-token time falls from 99 to 12 s. On twelve Mac Studio M3 Ultras it sustains 10,656 tok/s across 38,563 requests from 384 agents without a failure. Superfluid is available under the Apache-2.0 licence at https://github.com/basecompute/superfluid.

candidates.title: PHONON: Silicon-Photonic Network-on-Interposer for Energy-Efficient and High Performance LLM Inferencing
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit extreme compute and memory demands, necessitating large-scale multi-chiplet systems to achieve high-performance and scalability. In such systems, frequent off-chip memory accesses for model parameters and intermediate activation exchanges induce substantial data movement between compute and storage chiplets, making inter-chiplet communication a critical performance and energy bottleneck. Silicon photonic (SiPh) Networks-on-Interposers (NoIs) offer high bandwidth and low latency communication, making them an attractive choice for the inter-chiplet communication backbone. However, conventional SiPh NoI designs require long-range multi-hop data exchanges, resulting in degraded performance and energy efficiency, and poor scalability. In this work, we present PHONON, a novel Silicon- Pho tonic N etwork- o n-I n terposer architecture, that jointly optimizes compute–compute and compute–storage inter-chiplet communication. PHONON employs structured waveguide placement, cluster-level connectivity to storage chiplets, and optimized mapping of compute kernels to chiplets. PHONON optimizes waveguide crossings and reduces waveguide propagation losses, insertion losses, and memory-access contention. Simulation results show that PHONON reduces NoI latency and energy consumption by up to 9.4× and 28.4×, respectively, compared to state-of-the-art SiPh NoI architectures, enabling scalable, high-performance, and energy-efficient LLM acceleration. PHONON reduces the LLM-serving metrics of time-to-first-token (TTFT) by up to 1.48×, and improves tokens/sec and tokens/Joule by up to 4.9× and 28×, respectively, compared to SiPh NoI counterparts.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): Enhancing LLMs with External Knowledge
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) generate fluent answers, but they depend mainly on their training data. As a result they can give wrong or outdated responses, and they may lack the specific information a question needs. Retraining a model again and again to fix this takes a great deal of time. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses the problem by retrieving relevant information from external knowledge sources, such as documents, databases and the web, before a response is generated. This paper presents a literature survey and problem understanding for RAG. It explains the retrieve–augment–generate workflow, states the problem and six objectives, and relates RAG to current technology trends: real-time information, enterprise AI, agentic AI, cost-effective scalability and reduced hallucination. Eight studies from 2020 to 2026 are compared on methodology, key findings and limitations. The analysis reveals that the quality of information retrieval, as well as the effectiveness, accuracy and assessment, still remain unstudied topics. Four research gaps are identified: high computational resources, irrelevant or incomplete retrieval, limited effectiveness in specialised domains, and the need for better evaluation of factuality, relevance and reliability.

candidates.title: Large language model agents with simulation-trained surrogates retrieve multi-objective reservoir development plans from hierarchical knowledge graphs
candidates.abstract: Optimizing oilfield development is a high-dimensional, multi-objective decision problem: candidate plans must balance hydrocarbon recovery against economic return while satisfying operational constraints. Retrieval methods that rank evidence by textual or structural similarity cannot express such trade-offs or reject infeasible plans, whereas full-physics simulation is too costly to run inside an interactive search. We present PHARAOH, a framework in which a large language model agent retrieves development plans over a multi-resolution knowledge graph, guided by a simulation-trained surrogate model that estimates objectives such as ultimate recovery and net present value. The agent combines global anchoring with type-filtered hierarchical refinement and aggregates parallel search trajectories into a set of diverse recommendations; its policy is then distilled into a compact student model. PHARAOH screens and ranks candidates within a pre-built decision space rather than solving a continuous optimization problem. On PetroGraph, a benchmark built from three public reservoir simulation models, PHARAOH attains the best average performance among the compared baselines, improving Hit@1 by 8.8 and Recall@20 by 7.1 over a surrogate-guided non-agentic search. Full-physics re-simulation shows that 14 of 15 top-ranked plans satisfy the operational constraints, although near-boundary plans remain sensitive to surrogate error. The distilled 7B student retains about 85% of the teacher’s Hit@1 at a fraction of the inference cost. These findings are limited to three simulation benchmarks; field-scale validation remains future work.

candidates.title: Automating postmarketing pharmacovigilance with large language model agents
candidates.abstract: Postmarketing pharmacovigilance relies on spontaneous adverse event reporting and labor-intensive observational studies, which suffer from underreporting and delayed risk detection. Large language model (LLM) agents could automate real-world evidence generation, but generalist agents make ad hoc analytical decisions that compromise epidemiological validity and reproducibility. Here we present MedCheckpoint, a multi-agent LLM system for automated postmarketing pharmacovigilance. MedCheckpoint grounds each analytical stage in a curated, source-traceable medical knowledge base, locks core study-design parameters before execution, performs patient-level analyses with human-written deterministic statistical tools, and enforces checkpoint rules that abort infeasible analyses, with optional human-in-the-loop review. We evaluated MedCheckpoint using a 54-question benchmark on a dual-purpose simulated electronic health record (EHR) testbed of 2.7 million individuals, designed with reliable clinical signals to evaluate routine analytical accuracy alongside spurious signals to stress-test system rigor. Across the benchmark, MedCheckpoint outperformed two coding-agent baselines in report quality across five dimensions rated by three independent LLM judges (overall means 4.81-4.88 versus 4.25-4.55 and 4.02-4.29) and yielded higher run-to-run consistency (mean within-question standard deviation 0.116-0.186 versus up to 0.440). Crucially, while baselines failed on up to 2 of 21 runs when handling infeasible comparisons or unmeasurable outcomes, MedCheckpoint produced no misleading failures across all seven stress-test trap questions with known data limitations. MedCheckpoint enables reliable, auditable, and scalable pharmacovigilance analysis.

candidates.title: Human or Synthetic? What a Fixed Budget Buys for Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Post-training of large language models typically combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with preference-based fine-tuning such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Human-annotated and synthetically generated preference data differ substantially in per-sample cost, but prior work typically holds sample count fixed when comparing the two. In this work, we explicitly study the interplay between cost and performance by comparing the effect of post-training with human and synthetic preference data under a fixed, dollar-matched annotation budget. We train and evaluate multiple base model families across helpfulness and summarization tasks. We find that synthetic data is far more cost-efficient at low-to-moderate budgets, achieving high win rates with as little as \$200--\$400. On helpfulness, human data closes the gap only at budgets roughly two orders of magnitude larger; on summarization, it does not close the gap at any tested budget. We also find that human-annotated data varies in reliability: one widely used human preference source substantially underperforms another, and the gap persists even after standard remedies such as domain restriction and deduplication.

candidates.title: Multimodal retrieval-augmented generation for domain knowledge enhancement in large language models
candidates.abstract: Large language models are susceptible to problems such as lagging parameter knowledge updates, insufficient alignment of textual and graphical evidence, and incomplete factual basis for answers in domain-specific question answering. To address these issues, a domain-consistent multimodal retrieval enhancement generation framework, DC-MRAG, is proposed. This framework comprises four modules: domain anchor index, hierarchical cross-modal retrieval, evidence consistency fusion, and uncertainty-aware generation. It achieves unified representation of textual and graphical evidence through domain concept constraints, utilizes multi-factor scoring for candidate recall and re-ranking, compresses context based on evidence support, and controls generation risk through confidence calibration and selective secondary retrieval. Under a unified example experimental setting, the proposed method achieves an exact match rate of 84.9%, a recall@5 rate of 91.4%, an answer fidelity of 94.2%, and a phantom rate reduction to 4.6%. Compared to RAMQA, the exact match rate is improved by 4.2 percentage points, the phantom rate is relatively reduced by 41.03%, context tokens are reduced by 26.99%, P95 response latency is reduced by 23.43%, and throughput is increased by 28.85%. The results show that the collaborative design of domain indexing, cross-modal retrieval, evidence fusion, and generative calibration can improve the accuracy, evidence reliability, and online service efficiency of knowledge-based question answering.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Tutor for MOOCs: Comparative Evaluation of LLM Architectures
candidates.abstract: The use of Large Language Models (LLMs) for Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) presents new opportunities to facilitate context-aware support. In this context, LLMs have two main limitations: (1) the inability to provide answers relevant to the context of the student and (2) the risk of providing inaccurate answers. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has been designed to overcome these limitations by combining the retrieval of curated information with the language processing capabilities of LLMs. However, there is little evidence on how the choice of deployment architecture and LLM affects the latency, answer quality, cost and student perception of RAG tutors. This paper presents the design, multi-LLM evaluation and student perception of RAG-Tutor, a RAG architecture built to serve as a chatbot for MOOCs. RAG-Tutor was evaluated in an “Introduction to Operating Systems” MOOC across three deployment architectures and seven LLMs, using a benchmark of 196 expert-validated questions. An exploratory study with 30 students examined self-reported perceptions of satisfaction, trust and explainability. RAG-Tutor demonstrates the feasibility of RAG systems by showing that: (1) RAG approaches outperform stand-alone LLMs; (2) not all architectures provide real-time interactions and high-quality answers; and (3) the choice of LLM has an impact on student perceptions.

candidates.title: Enhancing capability boundaries of in-context learning in large language models for computer vision
candidates.abstract: Visual context learning enables large language models to perform visual question answering and cross-scene reasoning based on a limited number of image and text examples. However, its performance is limited by factors such as example redundancy, visual token overhead, insufficient cross-modal alignment, and prediction confidence bias. To address these issues, this paper proposes a boundary-enhanced visual context learning framework, BEV-ICL. It improves the task relevance and structural diversity of examples through boundary-aware example selection and rearrangement, preserves key objects and spatial relationships using structure-aware visual token compression, achieves dynamic alignment of visual evidence with question semantics through relational conditional gating, and enhances output reliability through uncertainty-aware reasoning and probability calibration. In the constructed experimental scheme, the average accuracy of the proposed method reached 69.6%, an improvement of 4.4 percentage points compared to the comparison method. The long context accuracy increased from 57.3% to 68.9%; the number of context tokens decreased from 5120 to 3200, a reduction of 37.50%; the average inference latency decreased from 428.6 ms to 286.4 ms , a reduction of 33.18%; P95 latency decreased by 34.29%; system throughput increased from 22.4 req/s to 33.8 req/s, an increase of 50.89%; and the expected calibration error decreased from 6.8% to 4.1%. These results demonstrate that jointly optimizing example configuration, visual structure compression, cross-modal relationships, and prediction calibration can expand the applicability of visual context learning in terms of task performance, context capacity, and inference efficiency.

candidates.title: DRAMA: Dissecting Attention Redundancy for Accelerating Multimodal Diffusion Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate text through iterative masked denoising with bidirectional attention, offering a compelling alternative to autoregressive vision-language modeling. However, each denoising step requires a full forward pass over long multimodal sequences in which visual tokens dominate the sequence length, and a fixed step budget further compounds this quadratic per-step cost. Existing inference acceleration approaches for multimodal dLLMs characterize attention redundancy implicitly, motivating designs from isolated attention visualizations rather than from measurement. We close this gap with DRAMA, a training-free acceleration framework grounded in a systematic dissection of attention redundancy in multimodal dLLMs. By probing attention tensors along spatial and temporal axes, we reveal two persistent redundancy structures: (i) attention mass consistently concentrates on a sparse subset of visual tokens, and (ii) attention distributions rapidly stabilize across denoising steps after an initial formation phase. These findings motivate two complementary mechanisms: Spatial-Redundancy-Aware Visual Token Pruning (SVTP) and Sufficiency-Guided Adaptive Stopping (SGAS). Together, DRAMA achieves an average 18.67 times inference speedup across six vision-language benchmarks without training, architectural modification, or attention caching, while maintaining competitive accuracy. Our results establish a strong, measurement-grounded acceleration baseline for multimodal dLLM inference.

candidates.title: Programming Quantum Circuit Parameters with Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated the ability to generate parameters for variational quantum circuits without conventional optimization. However, the conditions under which this approach is effective remain unclear. Here, we investigate a frozen, general-purpose LLM that generates complete circuit parameter vectors from symbolic circuit and Hamiltonian descriptions, with optional iterative energy feedback. We evaluate the approach on general random Hamiltonians, structured parent Hamiltonians, and molecular systems. For general Hamiltonians, LLM-generated parameters exhibit larger energy errors than conventional Adam optimization, while additional feedback generally provides limited improvement. In contrast, for structured Hamiltonians, the LLM can generate promising low-energy parameter configurations, suggesting that identifiable physical and mathematical structure facilitates parameter inference. We also show that direct LLM predictions of minimum energies can violate the Hamiltonian spectral lower bound, whereas generated circuit parameters allow independent evaluation of physically realizable energy expectation values. Finally, we investigate blind circuit interpretation and find that the LLM can predict measurement outcomes even when it fails to identify the underlying quantum algorithm. These findings highlight the role of problem structure, the limitations of iterative LLM optimization, and the importance of independently verifiable predictions in quantum parameter programming.

candidates.title: Large language models for mental health
candidates.abstract: Digital technologies have long been explored as a complement to standard procedure in mental health research and practice, ranging from the management of electronic health records to app-based interventions. The recent emergence of large language models (LLMs), both proprietary and open-source ones, represents a major new opportunity on that front. Yet there is still a divide between the community developing LLMs and the one which may benefit from them, thus hindering the beneficial translation of the technology into clinical use. This divide largely stems from the lack of a common language and understanding regarding the technology’s inner workings, capabilities, and risks. Our tutorial-style review attempts to bridge this gap by providing intuitive explanations behind the basic concepts related to contemporary LLMs.

candidates.title: Hyperbolic Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success and demonstrated superior performance across various tasks, including natural language processing (NLP), weather forecasting, biological protein folding, text generation, and solving mathematical problems. However, many real-world data exhibit highly non-Euclidean latent hierarchical anatomy, such as protein networks, transportation networks, financial networks, brain networks, and linguistic structures or syntactic trees in natural languages. Effectively learning intrinsic semantic entailment and hierarchical relationships from these raw, unstructured input data using LLMs remains an underexplored area. Due to its effectiveness in modeling tree-like hierarchical structures, hyperbolic geometry—a non-Euclidean space—has rapidly gained popularity as an expressive latent representation space for complex data modeling across domains such as graphs, images, languages, and multimodal data. Here, we provide a comprehensive and contextual exposition of recent advancements in LLMs that leverage hyperbolic geometry as a representation space to enhance semantic representation learning and multiscale reasoning. Specifically, the paper presents a taxonomy of the principal techniques of hyperbolic LLMs (HypLLMs) in terms of four main categories: (1) hyperbolic LLMs through exp/log maps; (2) hyperbolic fine-tuned models; (3) fully hyperbolic LLMs; and (4) hyperbolic state-space models. We also explore crucial potential applications and outline future research directions. A repository of key papers, models, datasets, and code implementations is available at https://github.com/sarangp2402/Hyperbolic-LLM-Models .

candidates.title: Evolutionary Trajectories in Large Language Models: From Transformers to Reasoning-Augmented Systems
candidates.abstract: The accelerated evolution of the Large Language Models (LLM) has taken natural linguistic processing to the next phase of transformer-based frameworks to more sophisticated tools, including GPT-3 and GPT-4. Regardless of the enhancement in fluency and usefulness that scaling laws and alignment techniques introduced, the issue of hallucination still remains a scourge of the flesh with models producing realistically false or misleading results. As a method of handling this weakness, there has to exist structured reasoning and checking in the LLM pipelines. The given paper explains the development of the LLMs into the reasoning-enhanced systems and evaluates the following strategies used in TruthfulQA: Baseline, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), ReAct, and Self-Consistency. The findings reveal that reasoning augmentation can potentially decrease hallucinations by up to 1520 and accuracy by 3040 percent compared to models that only use basic reasoning methods, which could be increased at the expense of increased computational latency. Sensitivity studies too demonstrate how incorporated tools and sampling would come in handy in providing factual underpinning. This paper provides the identification of tradeoffs between accuracy, efficiency, and reliability and the significance of hybrid verification pipelines in future LLMs.

candidates.title: CapLite: Prompt-Injection Defense for Small Language Model Agents without Model-Written Security Artifacts
candidates.abstract: Enforcement defenses against prompt injection, such as CaMeL, Progent, IPIGuard and DRIFT, ask the agent's own model to write a security artifact (a program, a privilege policy, a dependency graph or a constraint list) that code then enforces. We ask whether small language model (SLM) agents can be trusted to write these artifacts. Across 15 open-weight models, 13 of them between 1.7B and 12B parameters, they cannot: the policies, graphs and constraints that the agent's model writes admit attacks on 14 (Progent), 13 (IPIGuard) and 11 (DRIFT) of the models, and CaMeL's programs fail to run in up to 68% of episodes. We present CapLite, which derives its policy from the tool schemas, commits the write calls before any tool result is read, and admits a write only if every argument that decides whom or what it affects is stated in the user's request. This guarantees write integrity: injected text cannot add a write, and no write reaches a recipient, amount, object or destination that the user did not state. No attack succeeds in 13,935 attacked AgentDojo episodes. CapLite reaches utility under attack comparable to CaMeL's (29.0% vs. 27.2%) with fewer tokens than every other enforcement defense and than the undefended agent: 17.1k per episode, 18% of CaMeL's, and the highest utility per token of all enforcement defenses.

candidates.title: Agentic-Teacher: An Agentic Data Engine for Failure-Driven VLA Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Improving a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model requires demonstrations that address its weaknesses and provide effective supervision for learning. Coding agents can autonomously generate demonstrations through environment interaction, yet successful execution alone does not ensure effective supervision for VLA learning. We introduce Agentic-Teacher, an autonomous data engine for failure-driven VLA post-training. Given a VLA checkpoint, a task specification, and configured environment tools, the engine analyzes failed rollouts, selects intervention states, and iteratively develops closed-loop code policies through execution feedback. Validated policies become reusable demonstration generators that collect successful continuations from states where the VLA struggles. To make these demonstrations suitable for learning, Agentic-Teacher introduces temporally correlated action noise to broaden state-action coverage, removes idle frames while preserving gripper transitions, and filters trajectories using the frozen base model's flow-matching loss. The resulting demonstrations are combined with successful VLA rollouts for post-training, yielding an updated policy that operates without coding-agent assistance. Agentic-Teacher thus connects the weaknesses of a target VLA to both the generation and curation of its training data. In simulation, it improves $π_0$ success rates from 79.4% to 87.8% on LIBERO-10, from 80.4% to 90.6% on MetaWorld-10, and from 0% to 30.0% across three RoboCasa tasks.

candidates.title: Active Learning of Approximate LLM Ranking for Energy-Efficient Retrieval of Long Queries
candidates.abstract: Search engines and Large Language Models (LLMs) offer complementary strengths for document retrieval: lexical retrievers which rely on keyword matching are fast and energy-efficient, whereas LLMs capture semantic meaning and excel at interpreting long, context-rich queries. However, this comes at a cost that is computationally and energetically prohibitive. We propose the LLM Active Approximation Model (LAAM), a hybrid retrieval framework that introduces a lightweight learned predictor which serves as an intermediary between semantic retrieval and LLM retrieval. LAAM is refined through an active learning loop where an LLM labels a small number of documents. By concentrating LLM evaluations on the most informative documents, the framework substantially reduces inference cost while preserving retrieval effectiveness. We evaluate the proposed framework on TREC Robust 2004 using Lucene with BM25 retrieval and DeepSeek v3 as the LLM, under three levels of query verbosity. For verbose queries, LAAM achieves 87% of average P@10 achieved by DeepSeek's reranking (0.459 vs. 0.526), while requiring only 3.3% of the per-query energy consumption. LAAM is statistically significantly better than BM25 and is indistinguishable from DeepSeek on average precision, though not on MAP (Friedman test, P<0.05 with post-hoc testing). Overall, our results demonstrate that selectively approximating LLM relevance judgments through active learning enables retrieval accuracy to be controlled directly through the evaluation (and consequently energy) budget. Rather than committing to either inexpensive (and less accurate) lexical retrieval or exhaustive (and expensive) LLM reranking, our framework exposes a continuous spectrum of operating points along the energy--accuracy curve, allowing practitioners to select how to trade retrieval quality with computational budget.

candidates.title: VisText-VLM2Plastic: A Bilingual Benchmark for Visual Grounding and Environmental Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly support open-ended visual reasoning, yet their behavior in low-resource languages and sustainability-oriented domains remains underexplored. We introduce a controlled English–Bangla plastic-waste VQA benchmark comprising 402 image records derived from 136 base images and 2,412 question–answer pairs across five waste categories and three task types: recognition, visual description, and environmental reasoning. We evaluate GPT-4.1 mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-4B zero-shot using task-specific answer-quality metrics, bilingual consistency, and image ablation. Gemini 2.5 Flash yields the highest recognition point estimate, with 93.5% accuracy and 91.3% macro-F1. Across models, English normalized performance exceeds Bangla by 3.78 points on average, with the largest observed gap for environmental reasoning. Removing the image reduces normalized performance by 66.29 points for recognition, 52.89 for description, and 11.42 for environmental reasoning. The smaller environmental-reasoning ablation gap indicates that, in this benchmark, many environmental questions remain partly answerable from linguistic and domain priors. These results show why answer quality alone is insufficient for multilingual multimodal evaluation and motivate reporting cross-lingual consistency and sensitivity to visual evidence alongside conventional metrics.

candidates.title: Cited but Unused: Parametric Provenance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation systems attach citations to attribute claims to their sources. These citations frequently misstate provenance, and standard verification cannot detect this. We measure provenance by counterfactual value substitution: a fact in the retrieved passages is replaced with a false variant and the model re-queried. We find that across five sizes of one model family and a second comparator family, 1.2% to 15.7% of citable claims derive from parametric memory rather than the retrieved context. At the most conservative substitution distance these figures are 4.6% and 8.5% on the two models we tested at it, with the rate rising with model size within a family. We further find that natural language inference verification, the standard approach, gives results indistinguishable from chance across models, even when restricted to the cited passage. We determine that the cause is structural: a model answering from memory selects a citation that agrees with its output. Comparing ten attribution methods on identical claims, the contrast between the model's distribution with and without context best separates provenance. Acting on that signal does not improve provenance honesty at these base rates. The resulting detector is hence still not accurate enough to act on: it measures what the model knew rather than what it used, and separating those remains the open problem.

candidates.title: Maximizing LLM Utility While Managing LLM Fallibility
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can supply autonomous systems with plans, predictions, and judgments, but these contributions are sometimes wrong. This review asks how a system can maximize an LLM's utility while managing its fallibility. Our answer is to adapt the system's reliance on the LLM as evidence about the LLM's performance accumulates. Systems built from imperfect components, such as noisy sensors and faulty software, have long worked in this way, and the classical methods they use can be applied to LLM-based systems as well. A system can change its reliance on an LLM in several ways, depending on the LLM's role and on the other components in the system. Each change needs an estimate of the LLM's reliability, and the LLM's role and the kind of contribution it makes determine what to estimate. Classical methods from decision theory, estimation, and online learning then turn these estimates into reliance decisions. These decisions can reduce how often LLM errors affect the system. However, some errors matter even when they are rare. An independently verified mechanism can prevent such errors from being executed. Without one, adapting reliance using reliability estimates can still keep their risk within a bound. Studies on adapting reliance on LLMs are emerging but limited, and the reviewed comparisons suggest that adapting reliance can improve system performance.

candidates.title: Learning When Diffusion Language Models Should Regenerate
candidates.abstract: Remasking allows diffusion language models to revisit generated text, but effective correction requires knowing when and what to revise. Our diagnosis on Sudoku reveals two gaps. Hidden states contain error information that token confidence does not reliably expose, and remasking an isolated error usually reproduces it when the surrounding context remains fixed. These findings motivate DiVR , a verifier that predicts whether a partially generated sequence will reach a correct answer. Trained on the final correctness of the model's own trajectories, DiVR decides when to regenerate a block and which alternative to retain, while the generator itself stays unchanged. On five reasoning benchmarks with LLaDA-8B-Base, DiVR raises the average accuracy of the fine-tuned generator from 35.3\% to 43.4\% at $1.9$-$3.5\times$ the cost of greedy decoding, above search baselines that use $3.8$-$7.4\times$. It also complements post-training such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, and generalizes to other generators, including Dream.

candidates.title: Large language and atomic model: bridging atomistic representation and language reasoning for accelerating materials discovery
candidates.abstract: The combination of artificial intelligence and materials science promises accelerated discovery, yet existing approaches remain limited by a fundamental divide between physically grounded prediction and flexible reasoning. Large atomic models provide accurate structure-property relationships but are computationally expensive and lack general reasoning capability, whereas large language models excel at abstraction and inference but struggle with structured physical representations and reliable quantitative prediction. Efforts to bridge these paradigms have been impeded by competing training objectives: atomic models demand precise numerical optimization, while reasoning requires coherent sequential inference; when forced into a single objective, these requirements interfere, degrading both predictive fidelity and logical consistency. Here we introduce a Large Language and Atomic Model (LLAM), a multimodal framework with native structural reasoning capability that directly integrates atomistic representations with language-based inference. By aligning atomistic representations with the language embedding space through a lightweight cross-modal bridge, LLAM conditions both quantitative prediction and subsequent reasoning directly on crystal structures. Across diverse benchmarks spanning continuous property prediction and crystallographic classification, LLAM demonstrates strong performance while exhibiting improved reasoning capability. Case studies in optoelectronic-property interpretation, solid-state electrolyte optimization, and photovoltaic-material screening further demonstrate that LLAM can connect structure-grounded predictions with physically meaningful interpretations and application-oriented decisions.

candidates.title: Failure Recovery in Tool-Using Large Language Model Agents: A Structured Review of Detection, Correction, and State Consistency
candidates.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly act on the world through tools such as code interpreters, application programming interfaces, search engines, perception modules and robotic planners. Every tool call is an opportunity for failure: the model may choose the wrong tool, write malformed input, misread a returned value, trust an erroneous output, or leave external systems in a half-changed condition after a partial sequence of actions. This paper is a structured, qualitative review of how the literature detects such failures, corrects them and keeps the state of the agent and its environment consistent while doing so. It adapts the feedback-loop model and the loud/silent distinction of Sun et al. (2024) to organise a taxonomy of failures, groups detection methods into execution signals, output verification, model self-assessment, external critics and human oversight, correction methods into retry, repair, reflection, replanning, rollback and escalation, and consistency mechanisms into idempotency, compensating actions, checkpointing, action logging, state verification and memory hygiene. A study-by-study comparison of nine representative works, including 2025–2026 studies, records their methods, benchmarks, findings, limitations and treatment of state consistency. Within the reviewed corpus, explicit error messages are comparatively well exploited, silent failures appear to remain a major open problem, self-correction without external feedback is reported to be unreliable on reasoning tasks, and state consistency receives less attention than detection and correction. The paper closes with recommendations for evaluation and design and an agenda for future research. The review is not exhaustive and reports no new experiments.

candidates.title: SpaceMCP: Vision Language Model Spatial Reasoning via Model Context Protocol
candidates.abstract: Despite impressive advances in large language models (LLM), vision-language models (VLM) still exhibit limited spatial reasoning capabilities. Recent progress in feed-forward 3D reconstruction has enabled precise, real-time geometric understanding from visual inputs. In this work, we propose SpaceMCP, a framework that leverages these advances to introduce an MCP-style paradigm for spatial reasoning. Our approach augments a VLM with structured function calls, allowing it to query a scene graph for spatial information such as distances, object positioning, and camera properties. The scene graph is constructed in real time using feed-forward 3D reconstruction to recover metric geometry, combined with open-vocabulary segmentation to identify and localize relevant objects within the scene. Paired with the VLM's strong reasoning capabilities, the VLM is able to combine this primitive information to solve more complex spatial tasks. Without any training, SpaceMCP achieves state-of-the-art results on VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench and VSTI-Bench, outperforming recent spatially post-trained VLMs and improving its base VLM by 15-22 points per benchmark. We argue that, given the contrast between the relatively slow progress in native VLM spatial reasoning and the rapid advances in feed-forward 3D computer vision, this paradigm offers a promising path forward for enabling robust spatial reasoning.

candidates.title: Hybrid Retrieval for Retrieval-Augmented Generation using Vector and Graph Databases
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) supplements a large language model with evidence retrieved from an external knowledge source. Vector retrieval is effective for semantic similarity, whereas graph retrieval represents entities and explicit relationships that can support multi-hop and corpus-level questions. This paper develops a comparative framework for evaluating vector-only, graph-only, and hybrid vector-graph retrieval under a shared generation setup. The review covers dense passage retrieval, GraphRAG, HippoRAG, LightRAG, and evaluation frameworks for retrieval-augmented systems. A reproducible evaluation protocol is proposed around 50 stratified questions and metrics for answer accuracy, evidence recall, faithfulness, citation coverage, latency, and resource overhead. Because no query logs, model outputs, corpus, or annotation records were supplied for this manuscript, Section 5 uses clearly identified synthetic values solely to demonstrate how a 50-question analysis and its figures would be reported. These illustrative values suggest a plausible trade-off: hybrid retrieval may improve coverage of relational questions while increasing latency and infrastructure complexity. They are not empirical findings and cannot establish superiority. The contribution is therefore a transparent comparative design, a reusable evaluation matrix, and a set of hypotheses for a controlled experiment. A publishable empirical claim requires rerunning the protocol on a documented dataset and replacing all synthetic values with measured results.

candidates.title: Semantic Consistency of Vision Tokens: A Vision-Centric Perspective on Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: In computer vision, vision-language and self-supervised encoders are two unique paradigms characterized by global language alignment and high-quality vision-only patch representations, respectively. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often use the former because of language alignment, despite the recent rise in vision-centric tasks resembling traditional dense vision tasks that would likely benefit from the high-quality patch representations, raising the question whether self-supervised models could aid MLLMs in vision-centric tasks. To investigate this, we define semantic (in)consistency of patch tokens from language-aligned encoders and identify two sets of tokens, semantically consistent (SCTs) and semantically inconsistent (SITs). Through systematic probing via the removal of SCTs or SITs from the input of modern MLLMs, we show higher reliance on SCTs than SITs, as removal of the former induces larger performance drops. This demonstrates that MLLMs benefit from semantic consistency of vision tokens. With this in mind, we devise a simple yet effective extension of the MLLM training objective that combines traditional language modeling with semantic guidance via minimization of semantic inconsistency. This strategy, named Semantically-Guided Training (SGT), combines the signals of both loss terms to push the vision encoder towards providing semantically consistent tokens, while preserving language alignment. Extensive evaluation shows that SGT outperforms all baselines and MLLMs with specialized vision encoders on vision-centric benchmarks while keeping strong scores on text-centric benchmarks, thus setting state of the art on average across all tasks. Our results highlight the importance of combining language alignment and semantic consistency through the lens of MLLMs rather than independently from them and pave the way towards the design of better MLLM vision encoders.

candidates.title: Security, Privacy, and Trustworthy Design for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a language model draw on an external knowledge store. Factual coverage improves, but the system also gains security and privacy boundaries that a stand-alone model does not have: a malicious or unauthorized document can shape what is retrieved, enter the model context, over-ride instructions, disclose sensitive information, or trigger an external action. This structured narrative review synthesizes RAG attacks, defenses, threat models, and evaluation practices in work published between 2020 and September 2026. The evidence is grouped by pipeline stage, from ingestion, chunking, and embedding through retrieval, vector storage, context assembly, generation, output, and tool execution. Four findings stand out. First, poisoning, extraction, membership inference, and indirect prompt injection are distinct but composable threats. Second, attack success often falls when realistic chunking, re-ranking, corpus redundancy, and permissions are introduced, while adaptive evaluation can expose residual weaknesses in defenses. Third, credible security requires layered controls spanning provenance, access control, retrieval-time anomaly detection, context isolation, output monitoring, and tool permissions. Fourth, current benchmarks rarely evaluate authorization state, multi-tenant isolation, cache invalidation, deployment cost, or external actions. The review contributes a RAG security reference architecture, an attack-defense matrix, and a reporting framework for deployment-aware evaluation.

candidates.abstract: Background Multimodal large language models (LLMs) are rapidly expanding in radiology and digital health; however, their diagnostic performance across diverse clinical scenarios and fine-grained visual reasoning tasks requires systematic evaluation. Objective The study aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and fine-grained visual reasoning performance of 5 multimodal LLMs with bilingual medical imaging questions. Methods This cross-sectional benchmark study evaluated bilingual medical imaging questions using zero-shot prompting on 5 LLMs: GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Pro, Doubao, Yuanbao, and Llama 4 Maverick. Subgroup analyses by language (English/Chinese), question type (image/text), imaging modality (computed tomography, radiography, magnetic resonance imaging, ultrasound, and nuclear medicine), and anatomical system (neurologic, respiratory, cardiovascular, digestive, genitourinary, and musculoskeletal) evaluated intermodel accuracy and intramodel consistency. Image-based visual reasoning performance was assessed across modality, anatomy, lesion detection, and localization. Results A total of 298 questions (198 image-based, 100 text-based) were evaluated. Gemini 3 Pro achieved the highest overall accuracy (n=268, 89.9%, 95% CI 86.0%‐92.9%), significantly outperforming Doubao (n=235, 78.9%; P <.001), GPT-5.2 (n=233, 78.2%; P <.001), Yuanbao (n=216, 72.5%; P <.001), and Llama 4 Maverick (n=216, 72.5%; P <.001). All models performed better on text-based than image-based questions (Yuanbao, P <.001; Doubao, P =.02; GPT-5.2, P <.001; Gemini 3 Pro, P =.002; Llama 4 Maverick, P <.001). GPT-5.2 ( P <.001), Llama 4 Maverick ( P =.03), and Yuanbao ( P =.03) favored English questions, while intramodel performance remained stable across modalities (Yuanbao, P =.46; Doubao, P =.21; GPT-5.2, P =.26; Gemini 3 Pro, P =.96; Llama 4 Maverick, P =.45) and anatomical systems (Yuanbao, P =.82; Doubao, P =.52; GPT-5.2, P =.35; Gemini 3 Pro, P =.13; Llama 4 Maverick, P =.97). Despite near-perfect macroscopic visual recognition (modality and anatomy: 99.0%‐100.0%), accuracy dropped in complex tasks. Gemini 3 Pro outperformed Yuanbao ( P <.001), GPT-5.2 ( P =.002), and Llama 4 Maverick ( P <.001) in lesion detection (175/198, 88.4%) and outperformed Yuanbao ( P <.001), Doubao ( P =.004), and Llama 4 Maverick ( P =.004) in lesion localization (189/198, 95.5%). Conclusions Gemini 3 Pro demonstrated optimal, comprehensive performance and cross-lingual stability. However, current multimodal LLMs face a technical bottleneck in complex visual interpretation—particularly in fine-grained lesion detection and localization—emphasizing the need to prioritize local feature perception in future model development.

candidates.title: DiFiT: Distribution-Fidelity-guided Visual Token Pruning for Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Visual token pruning reduces the inference cost of multimodal large language models, but answer accuracy only partly reflects its effect. Pruning can change the probabilities of alternative response tokens even when greedy answers remain correct and unchanged. We compare full and pruned response distributions under shared reference prefixes. Average predictive drift grows with compression on fixed correctly answered samples. Separate analyses associate larger drift with more confidence-decision disagreements and sampling failures. We propose DiFiT (Distribution-Fidelity-guided Token pruning) to learn discrete selection from reference answers and full-token response distributions. Dual-View Distillation matches probabilities across the vocabulary, while answer supervision supports task quality. A learned scorer and differentiable Top-$K$ learn which visual evidence to retain. A multi-budget mask objective supports different retention ratios through one shared ranking over a frozen model. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, DiFiT reduces sampling-induced negative flips by 30.3% relative to FastV at 10% retention on four-task greedy-correct controls. It preserves 98.74% of baseline performance on MME at 30% retention.

candidates.title: TraceKV: Policy-Preserving Low-Rank KV Cache Compression for Reasoning Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Reasoning vision-language models (VLMs) impose substantial KV cache demands from both large multimodal contexts and growing reasoning traces. Low-rank KV compression has emerged as a promising paradigm that stores low-dimensional latents of KV states and can be combined with quantization. However, existing low-rank methods often induce growing predictive policy drift from the dense model when compressing reasoning KV states, resulting in reasoning failures. We identify two key causes of this degradation: calibration-state mismatch between static contexts and on-policy reasoning states, and unequal error sensitivity across KV states. To address these challenges, we propose TraceKV, a training-free low-rank KV compression framework that unifies on-policy calibration, sensitivity-aware SVD, and global rank allocation under a single policy-preserving principle, substantially reducing policy-KL divergence during reasoning. Experiments across multiple VLMs and visual reasoning benchmarks demonstrate superior accuracy--memory trade-offs, achieving near-lossless reasoning accuracy with 5.64$\times$ KV cache compression when combined with quantization. Optimized low-rank attention kernels further deliver up to 1.83$\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup. Code will be available at https://github.com/AK-DREAM/TraceKV.

candidates.title: How Far Can Frozen Vision-Language Models Go on Event Data? A Training-Free Study on EventBench
candidates.abstract: We present a training-free system for the EBMV @ ECCV 2026 challenge "Event Stream Understanding with EventBench" (General Understanding track), which evaluates vision-language models on five event-camera understanding tasks. We use none of the challenge's training data: our goal is to measure how far off-the-shelf, RGB-pretrained models can go on event data through representation and prompting alone. For four of the five categories (gesture recognition, detailed understanding, causal reasoning, and event OCR) we render event bins as red/ON, blue/OFF frames, select a category-specific subset of bins, stitch them into a single grid image, and query the same frozen Qwen3.5 9B vision-language model with a category-specific prompt for all four tasks. The fifth category, action recognition, feeds every bin directly into the organizers' EventGPT-Plus-2B. The system reaches 62.28% overall accuracy across 2,084 test questions (rank 9/27), led by action recognition and causal reasoning (80.27%, 77.22%) and limited most by gesture recognition and event OCR (54.70%, 34.57%). We visualize test samples from every category together with the exact images the model receives, score six alternative representations against the evaluation server, and analyze the full test set post hoc. That analysis shows that our bounding-box crop almost never tightened around content, so event OCR text reached the model at roughly one fifth of its horizontal resolution, and that detailed-understanding predictions are skewed toward the first two answer options.

candidates.title: SubGPU Pipelining: Intra-GPU Fine-Grained Spatial Parallelism for LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) decode is dominated by short, predominantly memory-bound kernels that make bursty use of on-chip execution resources and memory bandwidth. This paper introduces SubGPU Pipelining, a fine-grained, intra-GPU spatial execution model that cuts an operator graph into ordered contiguous segments, binds those segments to spatial stages backed by disjoint streaming-multiprocessor (SM) pools, and streams microbatches through the resulting schedule. Selecting the graph cuts, segment-to-stage binding, per-stage SM allocation, and microbatch size is a coupled optimization problem: each choice changes the overlap pattern, shared-resource contention, cache state, and execution times of the others. We evaluate SubGPU Pipelining through both simulation and silicon experiment using the GPT-OSS 120B workload with 32-GPU B200 deployment settings. The analytical shared-resource simulator searches across SubGPU pipeline structures and batch sizes to map the per-user/per-GPU throughput Pareto frontier. At matched per-GPU throughput, the modeled SubGPU frontier provides up to 2.2x higher per-user throughput than temporal execution, and at matched per-user throughput it provides up to 1.9x higher per-GPU throughput. To test physical feasibility and further validate the simulation results, silicon experiments are performed, using one B200 GPU to emulate a 32-GPU B200 deployment. The experiment evaluates one selected two-stage pipeline configuration at global batch 2,048 using CUDA Green Contexts and TensorRT-LLM kernels. Results show that SubGPU Pipelining improves mean DRAM read-plus-write throughput from 71.8% to 83.6% of peak, and reduces the 36-layer decoder iteration time by 10.33%.

candidates.title: Optimization of LLMs for Edge Deployment
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are known for showcasing astounding performance improvements over traditional machine learning approaches in various NLP tasks. When deployed on resource-constrained devices such as IoT endpoints (e.g., Bluetooth speakers, microphones), these LLMs with their high computational and memory requirements are not so suitable. This paper aims to explore optimization techniques for complexity reduction of LLMs without substantially degrading performance. Model pruning, parameter reduction, and early stopping techniques will be investigated. The study will evaluate existing lightweight models like TinyBERT and explore novel strategies for creating efficient LLM variants suitable for edge deployment. Metrics like model size, inference latency, and task-specific accuracy will be used to assess the trade-offs. The tradeoffs to enable practical LLM deployment in low-resource environments while maintaining acceptable performance levels are discussed.

candidates.title: Anytime-Valid Empirical Likelihood Inference from LLM Annotations with Adaptive Human Auditing
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to annotate unlabeled data as a fast, low-cost alternative to human annotation. However, their outputs can be biased and miscalibrated relative to human labels, potentially leading to misleading analysis and inference. We propose AAELI (Adaptive Human Auditing and Anytime-Valid Empirical Likelihood Inference), an online framework for estimating the population mean of human labels under a limited auditing budget. AAELI uses LLM outputs to guide adaptive human auditing and combines them with audited labels through predictable empirical-likelihood $e$-processes to construct anytime-valid confidence sequences. Our main theoretical result shows that a predictably learned efficient projection preserves the first-order profile empirical-likelihood statistic under adaptive auditing, without requiring a prescribed convergence rate for the projection estimator. This yields an exactly anytime-valid betting construction whose continuous-mixture form incurs a scalar rather than vector-dimensional mixing penalty. Supporting results establish adaptive empirical-likelihood asymptotics and show that a learned audit rule attains the oracle variance within the stated class of augmented estimating-equation designs under the same audit-probability floor and long-run expected budget. Experiments on synthetic data and three real-world datasets demonstrate that AAELI maintains empirical anytime coverage while requiring fewer human audits than the strongest competing baseline to reach a target precision.

candidates.title: From Search to Decision: How Post-Training Shapes Information-Seeking Capabilities in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Information seeking in large language model (LLM) systems increasingly involves decisions about when to acquire information, where to search, and how to evaluate and use evidence. Recent post-training methods have improved several such behaviors, but their objectives and evaluations span different tasks and system settings. This paper organizes research around six interrelated information-seeking capabilities and examines the learning signals, optimization methods, update loci, and credit-assignment mechanisms used to develop them. We synthesize empirical progress in targeted behaviors, end-to-end performance, search control, and generalization. Existing studies report gains in retrieval routing, query refinement, multi-tool exploration, evidence-grounded reasoning, and resource-aware search, although the scope of behavioral evidence varies across capabilities. We identify open challenges in estimating prospective retrieval utility, coordinating information-seeking decisions, and adapting to unfamiliar retrieval environments, and discuss evaluation practices for interpreting future progress.

candidates.title: Desalination LLM: Large Language Model Agents Design Efficient Graphene Membranes for Water Desalination
candidates.abstract: Graphene nanopores can, in principle, combine high water permeability with strong salt rejection, but finding pore geometries that do both usually requires many molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. We describe a design framework in which a large language model (LLM) grows a nanopore atom by atom, using pretrained predictors of water flux and ion rejection to judge each candidate. Two recent models, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, were tested with the same prompt and the same design protocol (30 steps, up to 30 trials per step, at most three atoms removed per trial, and a 90% ion-rejection floor). We wanted to know how much of an agent’s performance comes from the model and how much from the surrounding scaffold, so each model was run twice: once as a tool-using agent with access to the predictors, and once in conversation only, where it chose atoms and estimated performance without any feedback. Three scaffold-only baselines that contain no language model were run for comparison. With tools, both models stayed above the rejection floor at every step. Claude Opus 5.5 produced a single, island-free pore with a predicted flux of 122.3 ns−1 at 93.2% rejection, and GPT-6.1 Sol reached 131.7 ns−1 at 90.2%. Without tools the two models erred in opposite directions. Claude Opus 5.5 overestimated rejection and removed too many atoms, ending at 64.3% rejection, whereas GPT-6.1 Sol was overly cautious and recovered only 30% of the flux reached by its scaffold. A greedy search restricted by simple manufacturability rules matched or exceeded both agents in flux. Compared with the MD dataset and the deep reinforcement learning (DRL) designs of earlier work, the agents placed a larger share of their high-rejection pores above 120 ns−1. Taken together, the results indicate that predictor feedback, rather than the language model on its own, is what keeps LLM-guided pore design on target, and the six-condition protocol gives a simple way to make that attribution for other models.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation For Document Question Answering: A Review Of Retrieval, Embedding, Vector Search And Grounded Answer Generation
candidates.abstract: Abstract—The rapid growth of digital documents creates a need for systems that can find relevant information and answer questions accurately. Traditional question-answering systems rely on predefined knowledge bases or keyword search and may fail to understand the meaning of complex questions, while large language models alone can produce fluent but unsupported answers. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines information retrieval with the generation abilities of large language models. This paper reviews RAG for document question answering. It explains sparse retrieval with BM25, dense retrieval with dual encoders and sentence embeddings, approximate nearest-neighbour vector search, re-ranking, and the integration of retrieved passages into generation, including fusion-in-decoder and self-reflective retrieval. Practical issues such as chunking, context length and the tendency of models to overlook information in the middle of long contexts are discussed, together with evaluation of faithfulness and relevance. A five-layer system is proposed in which users upload PDF documents that are extracted, cleaned and chunked, embedded with a sentence-transformer model and stored in a vector database; queries retrieve relevant chunks that are passed to an LLM to generate grounded answers through a Streamlit interface. Research gaps, objectives and a comparison of retrieval methods are presented.

candidates.title: Comparative Vulnerability Analysis of Long-Context Retrieval Across Commercial and Edge-Hosted Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: While contemporary Large Language Models (LLMs) advertise expansive context boundaries reaching up to millions of tokens, empirical systems-level testing reveals that actual operational fidelity non-linearly degrades. In complex multi-needle retrieval and long-form analytical workloads, reliable recall routinely contracts to an estimated 20% of nominal capacity. This paper provides a rigorous comparative benchmark of six industry-leading architectures across both local edge-hosted open-weights deployments and commercial cloud environments. Utilizing a high-resolution, continuous 1% spatial depth tracking methodology, our baseline empirical testbed uncovers a critical processing anomaly on a bare-metal edge rig hosting a local open-weights model, exposing an abrupt 54x processing latency explosion (surging from ∼1.95s to 106.72s) occurring at the precise geometric midpoint (52% depth) of inference execution. To map closed frontier ecosystems without network noise, these baseline metrics are utilized as control parameters to initialize precise mathematical telemetry simulation matrices for commercial cloud platforms, capturing a downstream latency shift to the 88% boundary as context horizons scale to 32,000 tokens. Finally, we present an algorithmic, cost-effective middleware framework featuring dynamic semantic interleaving, high-attention mirroring, and vector-density position routing. Deployed within an enterprise production-grade retrieval pipeline, this architecture successfully mitigates intermediate retrieval failures by 42.6% and contracts commercial token billing consumption metrics by 31.8% without necessitating model re-training.

candidates.title: Chain of Physics: Supporting Fault Diagnosis with Engineering-Inspired Large Language Model Reasoning
candidates.abstract: Fault diagnosis in complex systems requires linking observed changes in physical quantities to the failure mechanisms that produce them. Experienced engineers perform this task by combining sensor information with knowledge of system behavior and fault propagation. Large Language Models (LLMs) can support this process, but their diagnostic reasoning depends on the availability of asset-specific engineering knowledge and on how this knowledge is represented and used during inference. This work introduces Chain of Physics (CoP), an LLM-based fault-diagnosis framework built around a Constrained Knowledge Graph (CKG) generated automatically from asset-specific reference documentation. CoP addresses failure-sensor association from textual engineering knowledge. The CKG stores diagnostic chains connecting failure modes, changes in physical quantities, and monitoring sensors. During inference, semantically similar graph paths are retrieved for each question and used as both information and in-context examples for the reasoning process. Candidate failure modes are extracted from the question and analysed independently through dedicated LLM calls, which generate plausible failure-to-observation chains. A final decision module compares these chains with the available answer choices. CoP is evaluated on the FailureSensorIQ benchmark across four industrial asset classes and three LLMs. Compared with direct prompting and conventional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), CoP improves diagnostic accuracy across all evaluated models, with gains ranging from 7.8 to 19.6 percentage points and from 11.7 to 18.2 percentage points, respectively. The results show that structured engineering knowledge can improve LLM-based diagnostic reasoning when graph retrieval is combined with in-context examples of fault propagation.

candidates.title: OpticalRAG: Pixel-Space Compression for Token-Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is bottlenecked by the token budget of large language models: feeding long documents into the context window is expensive, while aggressive textual compression discards fine-grained information that is irreversibly lost in a one-dimensional token sequence. We argue that this bottleneck is not fundamental to information density but to the choice of compression \emph{modality}. Modern visual encoders can pack the contents of a rendered text page into roughly a hundred visual tokens with little semantic loss, opening a new compression-fidelity tradeoff that purely textual methods cannot reach. We present \textbf{OpticalRAG}, a framework that renders documents as page images, encodes them with a frozen vision encoder, and distills the retrieved visual tokens into as few as $16$ injected tokens before passing them to the LLM. Two ingredients make this work without expensive cross-modal training: (i) \emph{Encoder-Bridged Retrieval}, which projects text-query states into the visual feature space of the frozen encoder, through a projection shared with the compressor, to retrieve visual tokens from a text query, with no contrastive training; and (ii) \emph{Query-Driven Distillation}, a lightweight cross-attention compressor that condenses the retrieved visual tokens into a small set of query-conditioned prefix tokens. On LongBench-v2, BAMBOO, and LooGLE-v2, OpticalRAG achieves the best compression-aware accuracy (CAP) on all three benchmarks while injecting only $16$ tokens, and improves the closed-book Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbone by $5.17$ points on LongBench-v2. Code is available at https://github.com/brighterr/OpticalRAG.
